For what is written, "he will be unclean until evening," can be understood to mean that he was no longer unclean during the evening itself but up to the evening, so that, cleansed, he could offer incense during the evening…

Sometimes, however, under one figure of either an act or an utterance, two terms may have one meaning. Thus the boards which were fitted together into the construction of the ark signify both the faithful and the eight souls who were saved in the same ark. Similarly, in the Gospel, in the parable of the sheepfold, Christ himself is both the shepherd and the door.
We find that arms have always needed faith, but faith has never needed arms. The rod of faith parted the sea which submerged the army bereft of faith together with its wicked leader.

Note how the teachers of the Old and New Testaments differ in their deeds but are paired in glory, for the one Wisdom issued twin laws in the two Testaments, so equal distinction gives the same weight to differing powers. Peter did not divide the sea with a rod, but then Moses did not walk on the waters. However, both have the same bright glory, for the one Creator inspired both the cleavage of the waters with a rod and the treading of the waves underfoot.

"The elite of his officers, who were standing three deep, he submerged in the Red Sea." Who are the elite of his officers? Surely those chosen by the devil for luxury, wickedness and pride, the source of all evil. Moreover, these, standing three deep, occupy those three ways in order to subvert man to evil deeds, to tempt him to evil speech or to win him to evil thoughts.

What then does Scripture mention in what follows? "In their thirst for water, the people grumbled against Moses." Perhaps this word that he said may seem superfluous, that the people thirsted for water. For since he said, "In their thirst," what need was there to add "for water"? Thus indeed the ancient translation has it. Why did he add this, except because they thirsted for water when they should have thirsted for justice? "Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for justice"; and again, "thirst is my soul for the living God." Many people are thirsty, both the just and sinners; the former thirst after justice, the latter after dissipation. The just are thirsty for God; sinners for gold. For this reason the people thirsted after water when they should have thirsted after justice.

Now let no one along with pagans or Manichaeans dare to censure or blame the justice of God. It is to be believed as most certain that not the violence of God but his own repeated wickedness and indomitable pride in opposition to God's commands caused Pharaoh to become hardened. What does that mean which God said, "I will make him obstinate," except that when my grace is withdrawn from him his own iniquity will harden him? In order that this may be known more clearly, we propose to your charity a comparison with visible things. As often as water is contracted by excessive cold, if the heat of the sun comes upon it, it becomes melted; when the same sun departs the water again becomes hard. Similarly the charity of many men freezes because of the excessive coldness of their sins, and they become as hard as ice; however, when the warmth of divine mercy comes upon them again, they are…

Moses performed no sign without the mysterious wood, for he received from the Lord a rod to work wonders and prodigies in Egypt. Moreover, as a sign that he had heard things divinely, it was said to him, "Lift up your staff." God, of course, did not need the assistance of a staff. But it was raised so that we might know how great was the mystery of that future wood which was prefigured by the shadow of this staff.

Moreover, as we are wont to sing in the hymn, "God is faithful, without deceit." For this reason, as I mentioned above, we should believe without any doubt concerning Pharaoh that he became hardened because of God's patience rather than his power. This fact we know clearly from his own admission, for when he was being punished he confessed in this way as justice compelled him: "The Lord is just; it is I and my subjects who are at fault." With what feelings then does a Christian complain that God is unjust, when even a wicked king admits that he is just?"

Behold true and perfect charity: he ordered the death of a few people in order to save six hundred thousand, with the women and children excepted. If he had not been aroused with zeal for God to punish a few men, God's justice would have destroyed them all.

Manna is interpreted as "What is this?" See whether the very power of the name does not provoke you to learn it, so that when you hear the law of God read in church you may always ask and say to the teachers: What is this? This it is that the manna indicates. Therefore if you want to eat the manna, that is, if you desire to receive the word of God, know that it is small and very fine like the seed of the coriander.

Then the Lord said to Moses, "Take the staff and strike the rock, that it may produce water for the people." Behold, there is a rock, and it contains water. However, unless this rock is struck, it does not have any water at all. But when it has been struck, it produces fountains and rivers, as we read in the Gospel: "He who believes in me, from within him there shall flow rivers of living water." When Christ was struck on the cross, he brought forth the fountains of the New Testament. Therefore it was necessary for him to be pierced. If he had not been struck, so that water and blood flowed from his side, the whole world would have perished through suffering thirst for the word of God.

Finally see what the Lord said to Moses and Joshua: "Remove the strap of your shoe, for the place where you stand is holy ground." Can this be understood according to the letter, beloved brethren? How could that ground upon which they trod be holy, since doubtless it was like the rest of the earth? However, notice carefully what was said: "For the place whereon you stand is holy ground." That is to say, Christ, whose figure you bear and of whom you seem to be a type, is holy ground. True holy ground is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ through whom everything heavenly and earthly is sanctified.

That staff, dearly beloved, prefigured the mystery of the cross. Just as through the staff Egypt was struck by ten plagues, so also the whole world was humiliated and conquered by the cross. Just as Pharaoh and his people were afflicted by the power of the staff, with the result that he released the Jewish people to serve God, so the devil and his angels are wearied and oppressed by the mystery of the cross to such an extent that they cannot recall the Christian people from God's service.

You are commanded to pull out the ass or the ox which is lying in the mud. Do you then see a Christian like yourself, who was redeemed by the blood of Christ, lying in the sewer of drunkenness and wallowing in the mud of dissipation and remain silent? Do you pass by and not stretch forth the hand of mercy by shouting to him or rebuking him or instilling fright in him? If he neglects to listen to you, mention it to the priest somewhat secretly, in order that he may accomplish by his authority what you were unable to obtain by your humble admonition. Know for a most certain fact that unless you first in secret and with great love admonish sinners and later publicly do so if you have been rejected, that sentence must be directed at you: "If you do not warn the wicked man about his wicked conduct," it exclaims to careless bishops, "I will hold you responsible for his death."

We should also know that the ten commandments of the law are also fulfilled by the two gospel precepts, love of God and love of neighbor. For the three commandments which were written on the first tablet pertain to the love of God, while on the second tablet seven commandments were inscribed, one of which is "Honor your father and your mother." Doubtless all of the latter are recognized as pertaining to love of neighbor. The Lord said in the Gospel: "On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets." Likewise we read what the apostle James said: "But whoever offends in one point has become guilty in all." What does it mean to offend in one point and lose all, except to have fallen from the precept of charity and so to have offended in all the other commands? According to the apostle, without charity nothing in our virtues can be shown to avail at all.

Original sin could not have easily been forgiven, if a victim had not been offered for it, if that sacred blood of propitiation had not been shed. Even then the words in Exodus were not vainly said of our Lord: "I shall see the blood and shall protect you." That figure of the lamb represented this passion of Christ our Lord. Blood is given for blood, death for death, a victim for sin, and thus the devil lost what he held.

When Abraham offered his son Isaac, he was a type of God the Father, while Isaac prefigured our Lord and Savior. The fact that he arrived at the place of sacrifice on the third day is shown to represent the mystery of the Trinity. That the third day should be accepted in the sense of a promise or mystery of the Trinity is found frequently in the sacred books. In Exodus we read, "We will go a three days' journey into the wilderness." Again, upon arriving at Mt. Sinai it is said to the people, "Be sanctified, and be ready for the third day." When Joshua was about to cross the Jordan, he admonished the people to be ready on the third day. Moreover, our Lord rose on the third day. We have mentioned all this because blessed Abraham on the third day came to the place which the Lord had shown him.

We have heard in the lesson which was read, dearly beloved, that "when Joseph was dead, the Israelites were exceedingly fruitful and prolific, and they sprang up like grass." What does this mean, brethren? As long as Joseph lived the children of Israel are not recorded to have increased or multiplied very much, but after he died they are said to have sprung up like the grass. Surely they should have increased and multiplied more when they were under the patronage and protection of Joseph. These words were prefigured in that Joseph, dearly beloved; but in our Joseph, that is, in Christ the Lord, they were fulfilled in truth. Before our Joseph died, that is, before he was crucified, few people believed in him, but after he died and rose again throughout the world the Israelites, that is, the Christian people, increased and multiplied. Thus even the Lord himself says in the Gospel: "Unless…

When the Lord handed over to you the land of the Canaanites, he said, "Take care, therefore, not to make a covenant with these inhabitants of the land that you are to enter; else they will immediately become a snare among you." Now we believe that by the grace of baptism all sins and offenses have been banished from us. If we afterward make a covenant with those same sins and vices, doubtless this covenant will become a snare for us because of our consent to avarice or dissipation.

The third precept is "Remember to keep holy the sabbath day." In this third commandment is suggested a certain idea of freedom, a repose of the heart or tranquility of the mind which a good conscience effects. Indeed, sanctification is there because the Spirit of God dwells there. Now look at the freedom or repose; our Lord says, "Upon whom shall I rest but upon the man who is humble and peaceable, and who trembles at my words?" Therefore restless souls turn away from the Holy Ghost. Lovers of strife, authors of calumnies, devotees of quarrels rather than of charity, by their uneasiness they do not admit to themselves the repose of a spiritual sabbath. Men do not observe a spiritual sabbath unless they devote themselves to earthly occupations so moderately that they still engage in reading and prayer, at least frequently, if not always. As that apostle says, "Be diligent in reading and…

It was not without reason, beloved brethren, nor without the signification of some mystery that there was a flame in the bush: "And the bush was not consumed." Indeed, the bush was a genus of thorns. What the earth has produced for sinful man cannot be put in any kind of praise, for it was first said to man when he sinned: "Thorns and thistles shall the earth bring forth to you." The fact that the bush was not burned, that is, was not seized by the flames, is understood to signify no good. In the flame is recognized the Holy Ghost; in the bush and thorns is represented the hard, haughty Jewish people.

Behold, the glorification of matter, which you despise! What is more insignificant than colored goatskins? Are not blue and purple and scarlet merely colors? Behold the handiwork of men becoming the likeness of the cherubim! Was not the meeting tent an image in every way? "And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain." Yet all the people stood around it and worshiped! Were not the cherubim kept where all the people could see them? Did not the people gaze upon the ark, and the lampstand, and the table, the golden urn and Aaron's rod, and fall down in worship? I do not worship matter. I worship the Creator of matter, who became matter for me, taking up his abode in matter and accomplishing my salvation through matter.

I say that they are gods, lords and kings not by nature but because they have ruled over and dominated sufferings and because they have kept undebased the likeness of the divine image to which they were made—for the image of the king is also called a king. Finally … they have freely been united to God and [by] receiving him as a dweller within themselves have through association with him become by grace what he is by nature.

The burning bush was an image of God's mother, and when Moses was about to approach it, God said, "Do not come near; put off your shoes from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground." Now if the ground where Moses saw an image of the Theotokos is holy ground, how much more holy is the image itself? Not only is it holy, I daresay, but the holy of holies.

This [cross] we have been given as a sign on our forehead, just as Israel was given the circumcision. For by it we faithful are set apart from the infidels and recognized. It is a shield and armor and a trophy against the devil. It is a seal that the destroyer may not strike us, as Scripture says.

"You shall make for yourself no molten gods." You see that he forbids the making of images because of idolatry and that it is impossible to make an image of the bodiless, invisible and uncircumscribed God. "You saw no form on the day that the Lord spoke.…" And St. Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, says, "Being therefore God's offspring, we ought not to think that the Deity is like gold, or silver or stone, a representation by the art and imagination of man."

Hold most firmly and never doubt that the holy Trinity, the only true God, just as it is eternal, is likewise the only one by nature unchangeable. He indicates this when he says to his servant Moses, "I am which I am."

In the first commandment of the Decalogue, just as the worship and service of the one Lord God is most clearly commanded, so for adoration and service to be shown by the faithful to any creature is most vehemently forbidden. For it is said there: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me." If this is taken as spoken simultaneously by the Father and the Son, the Father and the Son are believed to be one Lord God. But if either the Father is believed to have said this without the Son or the Son without the Father, it is necessary that the Father or the Son be denied to be the Lord God. Concerning this he said, "I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me."

And it is written also in Exodus that when the ruler of the land of the Egyptians with his warriors was pursuing after the Israelites and was already upon the point of engaging with them in battle, the angel of God stood between the camp of the Israelites and of the Egyptians, and the one came not near the other all the night. There is therefore nothing unbefitting in supposing here also that the holy angel who was the guardian of the synagogue offered supplications in its behalf and prayed for a respite, if perchance yielding to better influence it might yet bring forth fruit.
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 96

quotes.quote: But the Savior also demonstrated the great ignorance of the Sadducees by bringing forward their own hierophant Moses, who was well and clearly acquainted with the resurrection of the dead. For he has set before us God, he says, as saying in the bush, "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." But of whom is he God, if, according to their argument, these have ceased to live? For he is the God of the living; and therefore certainly and altogether they will rise, when his almighty right hand brings them thereunto; and not them only but also all who are upon the earth.
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 136

quotes.quote: And on the breast of the high priest were certain stones hanging, twelve in number, in the midst of which were placed two other stones, manifestation and truth. By means of a riddle through these the chorus of the holy apostles is clearly signified being, as it were, in a circle around Emmanuel, who is manifestation and truth. For he manifested the truth by having taken away the worship of God in shadows and in types.

And this is pictured for you in the writings of Moses. For the God of all came down in the likeness of fire on Mt. Sinai, and there was a cloud, and darkness, and gloom and the voice of the trumpet with a loud ringing sound, according to the Scripture. The notes of the trumpet were, it says, few at first, but afterwards they waxed longer and became louder and louder continually. What then was it which the shadow of the law signified to us by these things? Was it not this: that at first there were but few to publish the gospel tidings; but afterwards they became many?
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 60

quotes.quote: Such an enactment required a man not to injure others. Supposing him to have sustained an injury, his anger at the wrongdoer must not go beyond an equal retribution. But the general bearing of the legal mode of life was by no means pleasing to God. It was even given to those of old time as a schoolmaster, accustoming them little by little to a fitting righteousness and leading them on gently toward the possession of the perfect good. For it is written, "To do what is just is the beginning of the good way"; but finally all perfection is in Christ and his precepts. "For to him that strikes you on the cheek," he says, "offer also the other."
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 29

quotes.quote: And let us know that the law also of the most wise Moses is found to have commanded something of this kind to the Israelites. For a lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month, as a type of Christ. For our Passover, Christ is sacrificed, according to the testimony of most sacred Paul. The hiero-phant Moses, then, or rather God by his means, commanded them, when eating its flesh, saying, "Let your loins be girt, and your shoes on your feet, and your staves in your hands." For I affirm that it is the duty of those who are partakers of Christ to beware of a barren indolence. Yet it is a further duty not to have as it were their loins ungirt and loose but to be ready cheerfully to undertake whatever labors become the saints; and to hasten besides with alacrity wherever the law of God leads them. And for this reason he very appropriately made them wear the garb of travelers…
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 92

quotes.quote: The shadows bring forth the truth, even if they are not at all the truth themselves. Because of this, the divinely inspired Moses placed a veil upon his face and spoke thus to the children of Israel, all but shouting by this act that a person might behold the beauty of the utterances made through him, not in outwardly appearing figures but in meditations hidden within us.

As also the Word of God, when desirous [to establish the paschal feast] said to his disciples, "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you." Now that is a wonderful account, for a man might have seen them at that time girded as for a procession or a dance and going out with staves and sandals and unleavened bread. These things, which took place before in shadows, were typical anticipatory symbols. But now the truth has drawn near to us, "the image of the invisible God," our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Light. Instead of a staff, he is our scepter; instead of unleavened bread, he is the bread which came down from heaven; who instead of sandals has furnished us with the preparation of the gospel. It is he who, to speak briefly, by all these means has guided us to his Father. And if enemies afflict us and persecute us, he again, instead of Moses, will encourage us with better…

But the deceitful, and he that is not pure of heart and possesses nothing that is pure (as Proverbs says, "To a deceitful man there is nothing good") shall assuredly, being a stranger and of a different race from the saints, be accounted unworthy to eat the Passover, for "a foreigner shall not eat of it." Thus Judas, when he thought he kept the Passover, because he plotted deceit against the Savior, was estranged from the city which is above and from the apostolic company. For the law commanded the Passover to be eaten with due observance. But he, while eating it, was sifted of the devil, who had entered his soul.

For there was a command under the law that cities of refuge should be appointed, in order that they who were sought after to be put to death might at least have some means of saving themselves. And when he who spoke to Moses, the Word of the Father, appeared in the end of the world, he also gave this commandment, saying, "But when they persecute you in this city, flee into another."

Thus is it written: "The Lord therefore struck the people for their guilt on the occasion of the calf which Aaron had made." What greater and more manifest judgment could God have made regarding sinners than that punishment immediately follow their sins? Yet, since all were guilty, why was not condemnation visited on all? Because the good Lord struck some with the swords of his sentence in order to correct others by example and to prove to all at the same time, his judgment by correcting, his love by pardoning. When he punished, he judged; when he pardoned, he loved. His judgment and love were unequal: his love was more evident than was his severity.

Indeed consequently, "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed," as the apostle says. Offering himself to the Father as a new and real sacrifice of reconciliation, he was crucified—not in the temple whose due worship is now completed, nor within the enclosure of the city which was to be destroyed because of its crime, but "outside and beyond the camp." That way, as the mystery of the ancient sacrifices was ceasing, a new victim would be put on a new altar, and the cross of Christ would be the altar not of the temple but of the world.

For the name of Divinity is given for the highest honor in the world, and with whomsoever God is well pleased, he applies it to him. But however, the names of God are many and are venerable, as he delivered his names to Moses, saying to him, "I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial unto generations." And he called his name "Ahiyah ashar Ahiyah," "El Shaddai" and "Adonai Sabaoth." By these names God is called. The great and honorable name of Godhead he withheld not from his righteous ones; even as, though he is the great king, without grudging he applied the great and honorable name of kingship to men who are his creatures.

And when the holy One called Moses from the bush he said thus to him: "I am the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob." When Death heard this utterance, he trembled and feared and was terrified and perturbed and knew that he had not become king forever over the children of Adam. From the hour that he heard God saying to Moses, "I am the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob," Death [struck] his hands together, for he learned that God is king of the dead and of the living and that it is appointed to the children of Adam to come forth from his darkness and arise with their bodies. And observe that our Redeemer Jesus also, when he repeated this utterance to the Sadducees, when they were disputing with him about the resurrection of the dead, thus said, "God is not [God] of the dead, for all are alive unto him."

Fasting these forty days and nights holy Moses too merited to speak with God, to stand and stay with him and to receive the precepts of the law from his hand. For although this human condition prevented him from seeing God, yet the grace of his fasting drew him into close contact with the Divinity. For to fast frequently is a portion of God's virtues in ourselves, since God himself always fasts. He is more familiar, intimate and friendly with the person in whom he sees more of his works, as Scripture says: "And Moses spoke with God face to face like one speaking with his friend."

In this mystical number, I say, the children of Israel, arriving at Marah and being unable to draw the water because of its bitterness (for the well had water but no sweetness, and it was pleasing to the eye but polluted to the taste), drank water that became sweet and mild as soon as wood was thrown into it by Moses. The sacrament of the wood removed the harshness that the noxious water bore. I believe that this happened as a sign, for I think that the bitter water of Marah is the Old Testament law, which was harsh before it was tempered by the Lord's cross.

Let us also see if we are able to find Quadragesima's mystical number somewhere else in the Scriptures. We read that holy Moses fed the children of Israel with heavenly manna in the desert for the space of forty years. Good is the number, then, which always opens heaven. Good is the number, I say, by which Noah's righteousness is preserved and the children of Israel are fed. For this reason let us also observe this number so that the heavens might be opened to us in order that the rain of spiritual grace might fall upon us and the manna of the spiritual sacraments refresh us. For, after the fashion of our fathers, by this observance of Quadragesima we are both made righteous and nourished: we are made righteous by the washing [of baptism] and nourished by the sacraments [of bread and wine].

Yet they were also completely ignorant of the commands of Moses himself, who ordered them specially to eat this bitterness when he established the paschal sacraments for them to observe and said, "You will eat it with bitterness, for it is the pasch of the Lord." For he did not order, as they think, the consuming of the very bitter juices of insignificant herbs with the roasted flesh of a lamb. Rather, he commanded the fruitful devouring of the bitter words of Christ's precepts with the sacrament of the Lord's passion. For do not the words of the Lord seem to be bitter when he says: "If you wish to be perfect, leave all that you have and come, follow me?" And when he says that one is not to possess two tunics or a wallet or sandals, that bitterness of such words is a medicine for souls.

But the same Christ the Lord who did all these things now goes through baptism before the Christian people in the pillar of his body—he who at that time went through the sea before the children of Israel in the pillar of fire. This, I say, is the column which at that time offered light to the eyes of those who followed and now ministers light to the hearts of those who believe, which then made firm a watery path in the waves and now strengthens the traces of faith in the washing. Through this faith—as was the case with the children of Israel—the one who walks calmly will not fear Egypt in pursuit.

They arrived at a place called Elim, where there were twelve very pure springs of water and a multitude of seventy flourishing palm trees. See the mystery of God—how, after the bitterness of the law, the richness of gospel piety abounds. There the one spring is harsh to drink, but here the many are all sweet to imbibe. Once there was no refreshment after weariness, but now there is refreshment after labor. For springs are at the disposal of the thirsty, and palms are offered to victors. Palms are offered to victors, I say, because after the hardness of the law it is a victory to have arrived at the grace of the gospel. For part of the victor's reward is to moisten his mouth from a flowing spring and to take the triumphal palm in his hand. With the spring the confessor's tongue is purified, and with the palm the martyr's hand is honored—the former because it has praised the glory of…

[The Son of God's] cross is our victory, and his gibbet is our triumph. With joy let us take this sign on our shoulders, let us bear the banners of victory. Let us bear such an imperial banner, indeed, on our foreheads! When the devil sees this sign on our doorposts, he trembles. Those who are not afraid of gilded temples are afraid of the cross, and those who disdain regal scepters and the purple and the banquets of the Caesars stand in fear of the loneliness and the fasts of the Christian.

When Moses' hands were lifted up Amalek was conquered; when they came down a little he grew strong. The sailyards of ships and the ends of the sailyards move about in the form of our cross. The very birds, too, when they are borne to the heights and fly through the air, imitate the cross with their wings outstretched. Trophies themselves are crosses, and so are adorned victories of triumphs. These we ought to have not only on our foreheads but also on our souls so that, thus armed, we may trample upon the adder and the serpent, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory forever.

Yet there are also those who go out well and are blessed because they go out. I will show this too from the Scriptures. In Exodus it is written: "All," it says, "who sought the name of the Lord went out forth to Moses outside the camp." These went out well "outside the camp," because they followed Moses, that is, the law of God.

Let us therefore compare the divine Scripture itself with itself, and let us follow the path of solution which it shall have opened to us. For we find in the sacrifice of the Passover, which is commanded to be immolated "in the evening", a command similarly given that "nothing remain of the flesh until the morning". This is not idle, that the divine word does not wish us to eat yesterday's flesh, but always fresh and new — those especially who immolate to God the sacrifice of the Passover or "the sacrifice of praise"; it commands them to eat new and fresh flesh of that very day, and forbids yesterday's.

"You shall not leave any part of the lamb until morning, nor shall you break a bone of it: what remains you shall burn in the morning."

Just as the mysteries of the Passover celebrated in the Old Testament have been done away with by the truth of the New Testament, so the mysteries of the New, which we are to celebrate in like manner, will not be necessary in the resurrection; for this is the meaning of the "morning," when nothing shall be left over and whatever remains shall be burned […].

[…] "Imperfectly we know, imperfectly we prophesy," as the Apostle himself teaches, "but when perfection comes, that which is imperfect shall be abolished" — which corresponds to the burning up completely in the morning. For the night signifies the present world, and the day the world to come. This too the Apostle attests when he says: "The night is far advanced, the day is at hand."

Truly few are…

He who has crossed beyond the borders set by God on account of the disobedience in Adam is the Lord, He who has blunted the sting of death and cast down its power, and has given to the spirits imprisoned in Hades the possibility of leaping forth outside, through the proclamation of the good news; in other terms, He has offered a way of ascent to heaven through His ascension, when gates and portals were lifted up at His entrance: "Princes, lift up your portals, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter in."

And since the command was heard a second time by the powers that guarded the gates, at their reply, "Who is He?", they heard this answer: "The Lord strong and mighty in battle, the Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory" — Lord of the glory of the Father, in whom the Father is glorified. He "reconciled the world to Himself, not reckoning the transgressions…

One should also observe that the term prayer,which often differs in meaning from "invocation," is here employed in the case of one who promises in a vow to do certain things if God grants him certain other things. But the term is also used in the ordinary way. For example, we found this to be so in Exodus after the description of the plague of the frogs, which was the second of the ten plagues: … "But Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: 'Pray to the Lord on my account to take away the frogs from me and my people; and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.' " When Pharaoh employs the word prayer the habitual meaning of "prayer" is conveyed in addition to the above meaning. If anyone finds this difficult to see, it becomes clear in what follows, namely: "And Moses said to Pharaoh: 'Set me a time when I shall pray for you, and for your servants, and for your…

But Pharaoh resists; "the ruler of these darknesses" does not wish to release you; he does not wish you to be drawn away from his darkness and led to the light of knowledge. And hear what he says: "who is he," he says, "whose voice I should hear? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go". You hear what "the prince of this world" answers: he says that he does not know God. Do you see what raw pride does? So long as "he is not in the labors of men and is not scourged with men", for that reason pride held him fast. Then, a little later, you will see how much he profits under the scourges, how much better he is made when beaten. He who now says: "I do not know the Lord", afterward, when he has felt the force of the blows, is going to say: "pray the Lord for me"; and not only this, but even, when his own magicians testify, he will confess that "it is the finger of God" in the…

But also the oracles of the Lord, "the chaste oracles," are called "silver tried by fire." And likewise in another place the tongue of the just man is spoken of as "kindled silver." But the cherubim are called golden, since indeed they are interpreted as "the fullness of the knowledge of God." But also the candlestick in the tabernacle of the testimony was commanded to be set up golden and solid; which seems to me to hold the form of the natural law, in which the law of knowledge is held. … that gold is to be referred to the sense and the mind, but silver is to be referred to the word and to oracles?
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

quotes.quote: Some people give no thought to the question of demons, that is to say, to the fact that these demons, in order to be able to exist in the heavy atmosphere that encircles the earth, must have the nourishment of exhalations and consequently are always on the lookout for the savor of burnt sacrifices, blood and incense. Since they attach no importance to the matter of sacrifice, we would express ourselves also on this subject. If men who give sustenance to robbers, murderers and barbarian enemies of the great king are punished as criminals against the state, how much more will they be punished justly who through offering sacrifice proffer sustenance to the minions of evil and thus hold them in the atmosphere of the earth! And this holds true especially if knowing the text, "He that sacrifices to gods other than the Lord alone will be destroyed utterly," they nevertheless sacrifice to these…

Since "everyone who wishes to live devoutly in Christ suffers persecution" and is assailed by enemies, he who walks the road of this life ought always to be armed and always to stand within the camp. Therefore it is also related concerning the people of God: "the whole synagogue of the sons of Israel set out" it says "from the desert of Sin according to their camps, by the word of the Lord". There is, then, one synagogue of the Lord, but this is divided into four camps. For four camps are described as positioned around the tabernacle of the Lord, as is related in the book of Numbers. And you too, therefore, if you are always watchful and always armed and know that you serve as a soldier in the camps of the Lord, observe that commandment which says that "no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, that he may please Him to whom he has proved himself",…

But by the second plague, in which the frogs are brought forth, I judge that the songs of the poets are figuratively indicated, who, by a certain empty and inflated modulation, like the sounds and songs of frogs, have brought upon this world the fables of deception. For that animal is useful for nothing else except that it renders the sound of its voice with wicked and importunate clamors.

But after this, when Jethro had departed and Moses had come "from Rephidim into the desert of Sinai", and there the Lord had descended to Moses "in a pillar of cloud", so that the people, seeing, might believe him and hear his words, the Lord said to Moses: "go down, testify to the people and purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and let them be ready for the third day". If there is anyone who comes together to hear the word of God, let him hear what God commanded: he ought to come sanctified to hear the word, he ought to wash his garments. For if you bring garments here soiled, you too will hear: "friend, how did you enter here, not having wedding garments?" No one, then, can hear the word of God unless he has first been sanctified, that is, unless he is "holy in body and spirit", unless he has washed his garments. For he is about, a little later, to enter…

But that mention is made of locusts in the eighth place, I think that through this kind of plague the inconstancy of the human race, ever at variance with itself and discordant, is confuted. For the locust, though it has no king, as Scripture says: "leads forth its army arrayed in one battle-line"; but men, though made rational by God, have been able neither to govern themselves in ordered fashion nor to bear patiently the guidance of God their king.

How troublesome a trial it is to pass through the midst of the sea, to see the waves rising up in a heap, to hear the roar and crash of the raging billows; but nevertheless, if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, the waters will become for you a wall on the right hand and on the left, and you will find a path through dry ground in the midst of the sea. But that heavenly journey too, which we have said the soul makes, may perhaps have some waters as well; it may be that there too waves are found; for there is a certain portion of waters above the heaven and a certain portion beneath the heaven, and we for the present endure the waves and billows of these waters that are beneath the heaven.

And what after this? Moses is commanded to strike the sea with his rod, so that it may split apart and give way to the people of God as they enter, and so that the obedient service of the elements may serve the divine will, and that the waters, which were feared, being made "a wall on the right hand and on the left" for the servants of God, may not only know no ruin, but may even present a defense. The wave, therefore, is forced into a heap, and the surge, checked upon itself, is curved. The liquid takes on solidity, and the floor of the sea is dried into dust. Understand the goodness of God the Creator; if you obey His will, if you follow His Law, He compels the very elements to serve you even against their own nature. I have heard it handed down by the elders that in that parting of the sea individual divisions of the waters were made for each and every tribe of the children of…

And the briefly recorded fact that the heart of Pharaoh experienced a kind of softening when he said, "But you shall not proceed far; you shall go a three days' journey and leave your wives behind," and whatever else he spoke when yielding before the marvelous works makes it clear that these signs had some effect even on him, though they did not entirely accomplish their object. Yet not even this would have happened if the idea held by most people about the words, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart," rightly represented what was wrought by him, that is, by God.

"The chariots of Pharaoh and his army he has cast into the sea, the chosen riders, the three officers he has sunk in the Red Sea." Pharaoh, as one more powerful in wickedness and holding the kingdom of iniquity, drives "chariots." It is not enough for him to mount one horse; he drives many at once, he compels many at once with the blows of the twisted lash. Whomever you see more shameful in luxury, more savage in cruelty, more foul in avarice, more disgraceful in impiety, know that these belong to the chariots of Pharaoh; upon these he sits, these he yokes to his chariot, on these he is borne and flies about, and through the open fields of crimes he drives them with loosened reins. There are others, "chosen riders" — chosen, without doubt, for wickedness. But we have already spoken above about the riders; now let us also see who the "three officers" are. It seems to me that "three…

And it is added in what follows: "at evening", it says, "you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with loaves". And concerning this I would wish to know in what manner the Jews receive the sayings of the prophet. For what consistency will it seem to have, that either "at evening" they should eat flesh without loaves, or "in the morning" eat loaves without the addition of a relish? What of the divine gift, what of the tempering of the heavenly grace do you show in this? Is this the thing in which you place the recognizing of God, that the flesh at evening is eaten without loaves, and do you say that the majesty of God appears, if again loaves are eaten without flesh? But keep these things for yourselves and for those who, acquiescing to you, think that God can be recognized in the quails. But we, for whom at the end of the age and at the evening of the world "the Word…

"Leading them in, you planted them on the mountain of your inheritance." God does not will to plant us in Egypt, nor in low and lowly places, but he wills to plant "on the mountain of his inheritance" those whom he plants. Then, besides, that he added "leading them in, you planted them" — does it not seem to you as though he were speaking of children, who are led in to schools, led in to letters, led in to all learning? Understand, therefore, through these words, if only you have "ears to hear," how God plants — lest perhaps, when you hear that he leads in and plants, you should think that he is setting fig trees or other shrubs of this kind in the ground. Hear also elsewhere how God plants. The prophet says: "You transferred a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it. You made a way passable before it, you planted its roots, and it filled the earth. Its shadow covered…

Twofold is the house of the tabernacle of testimony or of the temple of the Lord. The first is that in which is the "altar of the whole burnt offerings", which is stirred up with perpetual fires, in which house it is lawful for the priests alone to stand and to celebrate the rites and ministries of the sacrifices, and to neither the Levites nor anyone else besides is access granted. But the second house is the interior one, separated from this only by a "veil". Within which veil are the "ark of the testament" and the "propitiatory", upon which the "two cherubim" are set, and the "altar of incense" is placed. Into this house "once in the year" whoever was first, the high priest, having first offered the victims of atonement of which we have expounded above, would enter, having both hands filled, one with the "censer of coals" and the other with the "incense of composition".… You have…

Whence it is said of them: "They were sunk like lead in the mightiest water." Sinners are heavy. Finally, iniquity too is shown "to sit upon a talent of lead," as the prophet Zechariah says: "I saw," he says, "a woman sitting upon a talent of lead, and I said: what is this? And he answered: iniquity." Thence it is, therefore, that the wicked "were sunk into the deep, like lead in the mightiest water." But the saints are not sunk; rather they walk upon the waters, because they are light and are not weighed down by the burden of sin. Finally the Lord and Savior "walked upon the waters"; for he it is who truly knows no sin. His disciple Peter also "walked," although he trembled a little; for he was not so great and of such kind as to have nothing at all of the nature of lead mixed within him. He had some, though little. On account of which the Lord says to him: "O you of little faith, why…

But what is it that follows? "The people thirsted" it says "for water, and they murmured against Moses". It might perhaps seem to be said superfluously, that he said that "the people thirsted for water"; for it would have sufficed to say that "they thirsted"; what need was there to add: "they thirsted for water"? The addition is not superfluous; for there are diverse thirsts, and each one has his own thirst. Those who are blessed, according to the word of the Lord, "thirst for righteousness"; and others no less say: "my soul has thirsted for you, O God". But those who are sinners suffer "not a thirst for water nor a hunger for bread, but a thirst for hearing the word of God". For this reason, therefore, here too he adds that "the people thirsted for water", who ought to have thirsted for God, who ought to have "thirsted for righteousness".

Now many have been troubled by the story of Pharaoh, in dealing with whom God says several times, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." For if he is hardened by God and through being hardened sins, he is not himself responsible for the sin; and if this is so, Pharaoh has no free will. And someone will say that in the same way those who are lost have no free will and will not be lost on their own account. Also the saying in Ezekiel, "I will take away their stony hearts and will put in them hearts of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes and keep my judgments," might lead one to suppose that it was God who gave the power to walk in the commandments and to keep the judgments, by his removing the hindrance, the stony heart, and implanting something better, the heart of flesh.

Christians every day eat the flesh of the Lamb, that is, they daily take the flesh of the word. "For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." And because the law of the Passover is such that it should be eaten in the evening, therefore the Lord suffered in the evening of the world, so that you may always eat of the flesh of the word, because you are always in the evening, until the morning comes. And if in this evening you are watchful and lead your life "in weeping and fastings" and in every labor of righteousness, you too will be able to say: "Weeping shall tarry until the evening, and joy until the morning." For you will rejoice in the morning, that is, in the age to come, if in this age you gather "the fruit of righteousness" in weeping and labor.

And we must eat the meat roasted with fire with unleavened bread. For the Word of God is not only flesh. He says, indeed, "I am the bread of life," and "This is the bread which comes down from heaven that one may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eat of this bread he shall live forever."36We must not, however, fail to remark that all food is loosely said to be bread, as it is written in the case of Moses in Deuteronomy: "He did not eat bread for forty days, and he did not drink water," instead of saying he partook of neither dry nor wet nourishment.
Now I have noted this because it is also said in the Gospel according to John, "And also the bread which I shall give for the life of the world is my flesh."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.99-101

quotes.quote: Finally, the unleavened bread too is commanded to be eaten with bitter herbs; nor is it possible to reach the land of promise unless we pass through bitter things. For just as physicians insert certain bitter ingredients into their medicines with a view to the safety and health of the sick, so too, with a view to our safety, the physician of our souls has willed us to suffer the bitter things of this life in various trials, knowing that the end of this bitterness gains for our soul the sweetness of salvation; just as, on the contrary, the end of the sweetness which is in bodily pleasure, as the example of that rich man has taught, yields a bitter end in the hell of punishments.

But we eat the flesh of the lamb and the unleavened bread with bitter herbs either by being grieved with a godly grief because of repentance for our sins, a grief which produces in us a repentance unto salvation which brings no regret, or by seeking and being nurtured from the visions of the truth which we discover because of our trials.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.102

quotes.quote: And of old indeed Moses said: "but I am ἄλογος (without speech or reason)" — which, though the Latin has rendered it otherwise, can nevertheless be more properly translated: "without speech or reason" —, and after he said this, he received reason or speech, which he had confessed that he did not before possess. But the people of Israel in Egypt, before it received the law, was in a certain way "mute", without speech and reason; then it received speech, of which Moses was an image. This people, therefore, does not now confess what it then confessed in Moses, namely that it is "mute" and ἄλογος, but by nods and silence indicates that it does not have speech and does not have reason. Does it not seem to you to be a confession of foolishness, when none of them can render a reason for the legal precepts and the prophetic oracle?
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 5

quotes.quote: But I will bring forward to you yet another thing, which you cannot contradict. In Exodus, where we in the books of the Church have it written that Moses answered the Lord and said: "Provide, Lord, another whom you may send. For I am of a thin voice and slow of tongue," you in the Hebrew copies have: "but I am uncircumcised in lips." Behold, you have circumcision of the lips according to your copies, which you say are truer. If, then, according to you Moses says he is still unworthy, because he is not circumcised in lips, it is certain that he thereby indicates this, that he is worthier and holier who is circumcised in lips. Apply, then, the sickle also to your lips and cut away the coverings of your mouth, since such an understanding in the divine letters pleases you. But if you recall the circumcision of the lips to allegory, and likewise call the circumcision of the ears allegorical…

So long as Moses was in Egypt and "was being instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians", he was not "of a thin voice" nor "slow of tongue", nor did he profess himself to be lacking in eloquence. For, as far as the Egyptians were concerned, he was both of a sonorous voice and of incomparable eloquence. But when he began to hear the voice of God and to receive the divine utterances, then he perceived his own voice to be feeble and thin, and he understood his tongue to be slow and hampered; then he pronounces himself mute, when he began to recognize that true Word which "was in the beginning with God". But that what we are saying may more readily be grasped, let us make use of a comparison of this kind. If a rational man, however unskilled and untaught, be compared with dumb animals, he will seem eloquent in comparison with those which are devoid both of reason and of voice; but if he…

As a perfect bride, therefore, of a perfect man, she has received the words of perfect doctrine. The first song, then, Moses and the children of Israel sang to God when they saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore, and when they saw the strong hand and the exalted arm of the Lord, and they believed God and his servant Moses. Then they sang, saying: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified." But I judge that no one can come to that perfect and mystical song, and to that perfection of the bride which is contained in this Scripture, unless he first walk through the dry ground in the midst of the sea … And by Moses I mean the Law and the Gospels and all the divine Scriptures; for then he will rightly sing and say: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

quotes.quote: We read that many songs were made in the divine Scriptures, yet the first of them all is this song, which the people of God sang after their victory, when the Egyptians and Pharaoh had been drowned. For it is the custom of the saints, whenever an adversary is conquered, to offer God a hymn of thanksgiving, as those who know that the victory was won not by their own power but by the grace of God. And as they sing the hymn, they take up timbrels also in their hands, as is related of Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron. And you too, therefore, if you cross the Red Sea, if you see the Egyptians drowned and Pharaoh extinguished and cast down into the depth of the abyss, you can sing a hymn to God, you can send forth the voice of thanksgiving and say: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified; the horse and the rider he has cast into the sea." But you will say these…

"The horse and the rider he has cast into the sea; he has become for me a helper and protector unto salvation." The men who pursue us are horses, and, so to speak, all who are born in the flesh are figuratively horses. But these have their riders. There are horses which the Lord mounts, and they go about the whole earth, concerning which it is said: "And your cavalry is salvation." But there are horses which have as their riders the devil and his angels. Judas was a horse, but so long as he had the Lord as his rider, he belonged to the cavalry of salvation. For along with the other Apostles he was sent and bestowed salvation on the sick and health on the ailing; but when he laid himself down beneath the devil — for "after the morsel Satan entered into him" — Satan became his rider, and, led by his reins, he began to ride against our Lord and Savior. All, therefore, who persecute the…

But if the mental voice of those who pray should not be extremely loud, though it is not weak, and should they not raise a cry and shout, God still hears those who pray thus. For it is he who says to Moses, "Why do you cry out to me?" when he had not cried out audibly (for this is not recorded in Exodus), but through prayer he had cried out loudly in that voice which is heard by God alone.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.101

quotes.quote: But meanwhile Moses cries out to the Lord. How does he cry out? No voice of his crying is heard, and yet God says to him: "why do you cry out to me?" I would like to know how the saints cry out to God without a voice. The Apostle teaches that: "God gave the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father!" And he adds: "the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings." And again: "but he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he asks for the saints according to God." Thus, then, when the Holy Spirit intercedes with God, through the silence of the saints a cry is heard.

After this the war waged with the Amalekites is described; the people is related to have fought and conquered. Before it ate bread from heaven and drank water from the rock, the people is not related to have fought, but it is said to it: "the Lord will fight for you, and you will keep silent". There is, then, a time when the Lord fights for us and "does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able", nor allows us, unequal in strength, to come to a contest with one "strong". So too Job at last, now made "perfect", completed that most renowned struggle of his temptation. And you too, therefore, when you have begun to eat manna, the heavenly bread of the word of God, and to drink water from the rock, and when you have approached the inner things of spiritual doctrine, expect a battle and prepare yourself for war. Since the battle is imminent, then, let us see what Moses commands:…

I think therefore, so far as I am able to perceive, that Moses coming to Egypt and bearing the rod with which he chastises and beats Egypt with ten plagues — this Moses is the law of God, which has been given to this world, that it may correct and amend it with ten plagues, that is, with the ten commandments which are contained in the Decalogue; but the rod, through which all these things are wrought, through which Egypt is subdued and Pharaoh is overcome, is the cross of Christ, through which this world is conquered and "the prince of this world" with his principalities and powers is triumphed over. And that the rod, when cast down, becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, who had done "likewise" — that the serpent is put for wisdom or prudence the Gospel word indicates, when it says: "be prudent as serpents", and elsewhere: "the serpent was more…

But I think this must be considered, that, whereas Moses spoke of the rest simply, he added to scarlet alone "doubled", and to fine linen "twisted". It is asked, therefore, why the other materials, by which the remaining elements are indicated, he named simply, but scarlet, by which fire is designated, he alone set down as "doubled". These things are difficult to understand and much more difficult to expound. Nevertheless, as the Lord shall grant, we shall attempt to explain. For some things must be spoken and some things kept in reserve. Let us see, then, for what reason he called "scarlet doubled". This color, as we said, indicates the element of fire. Now fire has a twofold power, one by which it illuminates, another by which it burns. This is the reasoning of the literal sense; let us come also to the intellectual meanings. Even in these matters fire is twofold; there is a certain…

Now let us see what "twisted fine linen" too means. For here also he gave something of addition beyond the other elements. We said that fine linen holds the form of earth, which is our flesh. He does not wish, therefore, the flesh to be offered to God floating in luxury and loosened by delights, but he commands it to be twisted and constrained. Who, then, is he who twists his flesh? Assuredly he who said: "I mortify my body and subject it to servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself become reprobate". Thus, then, is it to offer twisted fine linen also, to wear down the flesh by abstinence, by vigils and by the labor of meditations. Goats' hair also is offered. This kind of beast in the law is commanded to be offered for sin; but hair is a species that is dead, bloodless, lifeless. He who offers this shows that in himself the sense of sin is already dead, and that…

But one must not stand still even in this; the departure must be pressed on, the camp must be moved even "from Succoth," and one must hasten to come "to Othon." Now they say that "Othon" is turned into our language as signs to them. And rightly so, for here you will hear it said that: "God went before them, by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire"; you do not find this done at Rameses nor at Succoth, which are called the second camp for those departing, but it is the third camp in which divine signs come to pass. Recall what was read above, when Moses said to Pharaoh: "we will go a journey of three days into the desert, and we will sacrifice to the Lord our God." This, then, was the three days' space to which Moses hastened and which Pharaoh opposed; for he said: "do not go farther." Pharaoh did not permit the children of Israel to arrive at the place of signs, he…

It is difficult to see what this sign can symbolize for us. But since we must not stop seeking and must deliver to the reader what occurs to us as an interpretation, we will say that in many passages the hand is a symbol of deeds. Now the bosom of Moses has two meanings. The first, in accordance with the sense of the letter, makes the deed of the doer like snow, as it says in the Hebrew, and leprous. The second, however, in accordance with the spiritual law, shows that the conduct is pure and that it is restored to the will of the nature of the Word.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 32.268

quotes.quote: And after the people had offered, "Moses", he says, "called every wise man" for the fashioning, and the architect, that they might put together and fashion each of the things that are written. "But also the women", he says, "the wise women he called", that they might make the things which were suitable in the tabernacle of the Lord. You see, then, that all the things which are made are made by wise persons; both women are called wise and men are called wise. For "all the works of the Lord" are made "in wisdom". Each one, therefore, comes "wise in understanding" and makes the works of the Lord. It does not suffice for us if we only offer, but there is need that we also work with wisdom those things that are in us, that we may know how to mingle gold with fine linen and to double scarlet or to mingle it with purple. For what does it profit you, if you have these things and know not how to…

Why too does he blame Pharaoh, saying, "You will not let my people go; behold, I will smite all the firstborn in Egypt, even your firstborn," and all the rest that is recorded as being said by God through Moses to Pharaoh? It is incumbent on him who believes that the Scriptures are true and that God is just, if he is a thoughtful man, to take pains to show how God, in using such expressions as these, can be clearly conceived to be just.

And is there anything more profound to say of Israel, not of nature but of grace, of whom it was written, "Israel is my firstborn son," when Israel was in dispersion? You yourself will also understand that these are the scattered children of God for whom Jesus was to die in order to gather them together into one.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 28.185

quotes.quote: After this Moses comes to the mountain of God, and there Jethro his father-in-law meets him. And he "went out to meet him" from the camp, and does not lead him to the mountain of God, but "leads him to his own tent". For the priest of Midian could not go up to the mountain of God, nor could he go down into Egypt—neither he himself nor the wife of Moses—but now he comes to him with his sons. For no one can go down into Egypt and undergo the Egyptian contests, unless he be an approved athlete and such a one as the Apostle describes, that: "everyone who strives in the contest is temperate in all things; and they indeed, that they may receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible one. I therefore run thus, not as toward something uncertain; I fight thus, not as one beating the air". Moses, then, because he was a great and mighty athlete, went down into Egypt, went down to the…

"You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. The whole assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it at sunset, and they shall take some of its blood and place it upon the two doorposts and upon the lintel of every dwelling in which they shall eat of the lambs, among them" […].

We are given the command to sacrifice the lamb at sunset because in the last hour the true lamb, our own, the Savior, came into the world […].

We sacrifice and anoint with the blood our own houses — by which I mean our bodies. This anointing is precisely our faith in Him, through which we believe that the power of the destroyer is brought to nothing.

"The whole multitude of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening." The whole multitude of the children of the man who sees God, that is, of the power of God; at evening, that is, at the end of the times.

"And they shall anoint with its blood the lintels and both the doorposts of the doors." The lintels: that which is above the head of all the lambs; the doorposts of the doors: their edges, through which they enter and go out among them — some enter into them, others go out from them — in which are contained those who dwell among them.

The sacrifice takes place in Egypt, where Pharaoh reigns, a land turned toward the things of the earth and blinded by darkness, which is ignorance. Those live in the gross ignorance of their blindness who are subject to the lordship of him who is king in Egypt; and this man, who has fixed his dwelling there, is under the dominion of the…

For Aaron also "met" Moses, and he went out of Egypt. But "he met" him where, in what kind of place? For it matters where "he meets" him—Moses, that is, whose mouth is to be opened by God. "He met him," he says, "in the mountain of God". You see that his mouth is deservedly opened, who is able to "meet in the mountain of God". Peter and James and John ascended the mountain of God, that they might be counted worthy to see Jesus transfigured and to see Moses with him and Elijah in glory. And you too, therefore, unless you ascend to "the mountain of God" and there "meet" Moses—that is, unless you ascend to the lofty sense of the law, unless you win your way up to the summit of spiritual understanding—your mouth is not opened by the Lord. If you stand in the lowly place of the letter and bind the text of the history to Jewish narratives, you have not met Moses "in the mountain of God", nor…

See whether it is for this reason that God hardens the heart of Pharaoh, so that at a moment when he was not hardened he could say, "The Lord is just: I and my people are wicked." His heart has to be hardened further, and he has to suffer more, that he may not, because he has been freed of his hardheartedness too quickly, think too lightly of that hardheartedness and so may have to have his heart hardened over and over again.

For the Word of God becomes all these things to each one, according as the measure or the desire of the partaker demands: even as the manna also, though it was a single food, yet rendered to each one the flavor of his own desire. He offers himself, then, not only as bread to the hungry and wine to the thirsty, but also, to those who wish to take delight, he presents himself as fragrant fruits.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 3

quotes.quote: After the crossing of the Red Sea and the hidden things of its great and magnificent mystery, after the choruses and the timbrels, after the triumphal hymns, one comes to Marah. Now the water of Marah was bitter, and the people could not drink it. Why then, after such great and such magnificent wonders, is the people of God brought to bitter waters and the peril of thirst? For it says: "and the children of Israel came to Marah, and they could not drink the water from Marah, because it was bitter; and for this reason the name of that place was called bitterness". But what does it add after these things? "Moses", it says, "cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a tree, and he cast it into the water, and the water was made sweet. And there", it says, "God set for him ordinances of righteousness and judgments". There, where there was bitterness, where there was thirst, and what is…

But if, following Moses—that is, the Law of God—you make this journey, the Egyptian indeed pursues and hounds you, but see what happens: "the angel of the Lord," it says, "who went before the camp of Israel, raised himself up and went behind them. And the pillar of cloud also lifted itself from before their face, and stood behind them, and entered between the camp of the Egyptians and of the Israelites." This "pillar of cloud" is made a wall for the people of God, but upon the Egyptians it imposes obscurity and darkness. For the pillar of fire is not transferred to the Egyptians, that they may see the light, but they remain in darkness, because "they loved darkness rather than light."

"They went down into the deep like a stone." Why did "they go down into the deep like a stone"? Because they were not such "stones as those from which sons of Abraham could be raised up," but such as loved the deep and cherished the liquid element — that is, who seized the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things.

It seems to me that each utterance of divine Scripture is like some kind of seed, whose nature is this: that when it has been cast into the earth, it is regenerated into an ear of grain or into whatever other form of its own kind, and is spread abroad manifold — and the more abundantly, the more either a skilled farmer expends greater labor upon the seeds, or grants the benefit of more fertile soil. So then it comes about that by diligent cultivation a tiny "seed", for example "of mustard, which is the least of all, becomes greater than all herbs and turns into a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches". So too this utterance, which has now been read to us from the divine volumes, if it finds a skilled and diligent husbandman — though at first touch it may seem meager and brief — once it begins to be cultivated and to be handled with spiritual art, grows into a…

Thus I understand also that which God says: "Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?" There is an eye of the body, with which we behold these earthly things, an eye according to the sense of the flesh, of which the Scripture says: "walking vainly, puffed up by the sense of the flesh". To this we have another, contrary and better, that savors of divine things; and because it was blind in us, Jesus came to make it see, that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might be made blind.
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

quotes.quote: According to these things, therefore, God is perhaps said also to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh, namely because the material of his heart was such that it received the presence of the Sun of justice not on that side by which it illumines, but on that by which it burns and hardens: on this account, without doubt, that he too was afflicting the life of the Hebrews in hard works, and was making them work with clay and brick. … And as this visible sun binds fast and hardens the material of clay, so the Sun of justice, by these same rays with which he was illumining the people of Israel, was hardening the heart of Pharaoh, in which were clayey thoughts, according to the very qualities of its own motions.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

quotes.quote: In Egypt were the children of Israel; they were afflicted in the works of Pharaoh the king with clay and brick, until, groaning, they cried out to the Lord, and He, hearing their groaning, sent to them His word through Moses and led them out of Egypt. And we too, therefore, when we were in Egypt — I mean in the errors of this world and in the darkness of ignorance, working the works of the devil in the desires and pleasures of the flesh — the Lord had mercy on our affliction and sent His Word, His only-begotten Son, to rescue us from the ignorance of error and lead us to the light of the divine law.

For though there were three sons of Korah whose names we find in the book of Exodus—Aser, which is, by interpretation, "instruction," and the second Elkana, which is translated "possession of God," and the third Abiasaph, which in the Greek tongue might be rendered "congregation of the father"—yet the prophecies were not divided but were both spoken and written by one spirit and one voice and one soul, which worked in true harmony. And the three speak as one, "As the hart pants after the springs of the water, so pants my soul after you, O God."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 14.1

quotes.quote: Moreover it was said to Moses himself, "See that you make all things according to the form and likeness which was shown to you in the mount." It seems to me, therefore, that … in this earth the law was a kind of schoolmaster to those who by it were appointed to be led to Christ and to be instructed and trained in order that after their training in the law they might be able with greater facility to receive the more perfect precepts of Christ. So also that other earth, when it receives all the saints, first imbues and educates them in the precepts of the true and eternal law in order that they may with greater facility accept the precepts of heaven which are perfect and to which nothing can ever be added. And in heaven will truly exist what is called the "eternal gospel" and the Testament that is always new, which can never grow old.

Watch therefore, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. Not giving "sleep to the eyes" of our soul nor "slumber to the eyelids," so that we may await either our own end or the end of the age, whether that we should depart from this life or that this world should be brought to its consummation for us.

But someone will ask how the Lord, established as present among the disciples, speaks thus, as though not present but about to come, saying to them: watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. And the one who is more simple will say that he spoke this discourse concerning the second coming, in which he was to come. But another will say that he was speaking of the intelligible coming of the Word, still to come into the understanding of the disciples, because it was not yet in their understanding in the way it was going to be: since (as he shows through this…

We say, lest perhaps also the "palpable darkness" in Egypt was made in this manner for "three days", not from an eclipse of the sun, but either because dark clouds ran together into one, or because the air there then became thicker over the Egyptians only — for "to all the sons of Israel", as the scripture testifies, "there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling".

For it is also impossible in an eclipse of the sun, which happens from the coming together of the moon to the sun, for darkness to be made for "three" continuous "days"; and it would be believed that there was some other cause of the darkness in Egypt, if the sun had even been named, or as though darkened at that time. But now the scripture of Exodus says nothing else except that "Moses stretched out his hand to heaven, and there was darkness and gloom and the rest over the whole land of Egypt for three days;…

The ninth plague is darkness, whether so that the blindness of their mind may be convicted, or so that they may understand that the reasons of the divine dispensation and providence are most obscure. For "God has made darkness his hiding-place", which they, desiring boldly and rashly to search out, and asserting one thing from another, have been rolled down into the thick and "palpable darkness" of errors.

Moses, when he had come to the place that God showed him, is not permitted to ascend, but before that it is said to him: "loose the strap of the sandal from your feet." To Abraham none of these things is said, nor to Isaac, but they ascend and do not put off their sandals. In which perhaps this is the reason: that Moses, although he was "great," yet was coming from Egypt, and there were certain bonds of mortality knotted to his feet. But Abraham and Isaac have none of these things, but come to the place.

Finally it is thus also written that those who were unfaithful, "kept", it says, "of the manna, and worms bubbled up out of it, and it rotted". But that which was laid up for the sabbath day was not corrupted, nor "did worms bubble up in it", but it remained whole. And you therefore, if you treasure up only for the sake of the present life and for the love of the world, immediately "worms bubble up". How do "worms bubble up"? Hear concerning sinners and those who love the present world, what the prophet's sentence is: "their worm", it says, "shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched". These are the worms which greed produces, these are the worms which the blind desire of riches produces for those who have money and, seeing their brothers in need, "shut up their bowels from them". For this reason the Apostle also says: "but charge the rich of this world not to be proud in mind…

Let us now see also what follows, how the "sins of the fathers" are said to be repaid "upon the sons unto the third and fourth generation". For in this saying the heretics are wont to jeer at us, that it is not the saying of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another. But even according to their own reasoning, who say that the God who commanded these things in the law is, though not good, yet just, not even they can show how, according to their own sense of justice, it seems to accord that one should be punished when another sins. It remains, therefore, that we beseech the Lord to show us how these precepts accord with a just and good God. We have often said already that the divine Scriptures speak not everything to the outer man, but very much to the inner. Our inner man, therefore, is said either to have God as father, if he lives according to God and does the…

"Joseph died", it says, "and all his brothers and all that generation. But the sons of Israel grew and were multiplied, and were spread abroad in a great multitude, and grew exceedingly strong; for the land multiplied them". As long as Joseph lived, it is not reported that the sons of Israel were multiplied, nor is anything at all mentioned in these matters concerning increases and multitude. I, believing the words of my Lord Jesus Christ, do not think that in the Law and the prophets even "one iota or one tittle" is empty of mysteries, nor do I think that "any of these things can pass away until all be accomplished". But since we are of meager capacity, let us now knock only at those things by which we may proceed more safely. Before our Joseph died — he who was sold for thirty pieces of silver by one of his brothers, Judah — the sons of Israel were very few. But when for all men He…

But on the "tenth day of the seventh month" is this solemnity of atonement. "On this" day alone the high priest is clothed with all the priestly garments, then he is clothed with "manifestation and truth", then he enters into those inaccessible places, whither it is permitted to approach only "once in the year", that is, into the "holy of holies".
