For "once in the year" the high priest, leaving the people, enters into that place where is the "propitiatory" and above the "propitiatory" the "cherubim", where is also the "ark of testimony" and the "altar of incense", whither it is lawful for no one to enter except the high priest alone. If therefore I consider my true "high priest" the Lord "Jesus" Christ, how, placed in the flesh, he was with the people throughout the whole year, that year of which he himself says: "he sent me to evangelize the poor and to proclaim the acceptable year of…

But what does he yet add in his answers? "Why," he says, "O Moses and Aaron, do you turn my people away from their works? Depart, each one of you to your work". So long as the people is with him and works "mud" and "brick", so long as it is occupied in "straw", he does not think it perverted, but that it walks in the right path. But if it should say: I wish to go "the way of three days" and "to serve the Lord", he says that the people is perverted by Moses and Aaron. This indeed "was said to the ancients". But even today, if Moses and Aaron—that is, the prophetic and the priestly word—should rouse the soul to the service of God, invite it to go out of the world, to renounce all that it possesses, to give heed to the divine law and follow the word of God, immediately you will hear it said by those who are of one mind with Pharaoh and his friends: 'see how men are seduced and…

After these things: "and the men", he says, "took from their women, all to whom it seemed good in their understanding, and brought gems and earrings and rings and hair-clasps and armlets". You see here too how those bring gifts to God who see with the heart, who conceive understanding in the heart, who have the mind intent and devoted to the word of God. These, then, bring gifts, and they bring them even from their women: "earrings", he says, "and gems and armlets". We have already often said that, according to the allegorical interpretation, the woman is taken as the flesh and the man as the rational sense. Good, therefore, are these women who obey their husbands; good is the flesh which no longer fights against the spirit, but complies and consents, and therefore "if two or three of you agree, concerning whatever thing you shall ask, it shall be done for you", the Lord said. They…

But after this, when Pharaoh saw that through the midwives he could not slay the males of Israel: "he commanded," it says, "all the people, saying: every male whatsoever that shall be born to the Hebrews, cast into the river, and every female let live." See what "the prince of this world" commands his own, that they may seize our infants, that they may cast them into the river, and, lying in wait for the very first birth of our own, may straightway, as soon as they have touched the first breasts of the church, rush upon them, tear them away, persecute them, and overwhelm them with the waves and billows of this age. "See what you hear"; the wisdom of God through Solomon says: "understand intelligently the things that are set before you." See, as soon as you are born — nay rather, as soon as you are reborn — what threatens you. This is that which you read in the Gospel, that Jesus, as…

But also the "princes", he says, "offered" their gifts. What are these gifts which the princes offer? "Gems", he says, "they offered, emerald stones and stones of filling and stones for the shoulder-piece". Stones of filling are called those which are placed in the oracle, that is, which are set on the breast of the high priest, inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel. This which is called the oracle, that is, the rational, which is set on the breast of the high priest, has the form of the rational sense which is in us. In this are said to be placed the "stones of filling", which yet cling and are connected to the shoulder stones and are held bound together by these. The adornment of the shoulder-piece is a token of good deeds. Deeds, therefore, are joined with reason and reason with deeds, so that there may be a harmony in both: "for he who shall do and teach, he shall be…

But Moses himself too says to the Lord: "from the time I spoke with Pharaoh, he has afflicted your people". For it is certain that, before the word of God is heard, before the divine preaching is made known, there is no tribulation, there is no temptation, because, unless the trumpet sound, battle is not joined; but when the trumpet of preaching has given the signal of war, there affliction follows, there all the fighting of tribulations rises up. From the time Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God is afflicted. From the time the word of God is brought into your soul, of necessity a struggle is stirred up within you, of the virtues against the vices; but before the word came which would rebuke, the vices endured within you in peace; but when the word of God began to make the distinction of each, then a great disturbance rises up and war is born without treaty.…

In accordance with this we also note that saying: "The barren has borne seven, and she who was fruitful in children has grown weak." And as it is said among the blessings: "There shall not be among you one without children nor a barren woman." Therefore, if these things are so, just as there is said to be a certain carnal love, which the poets have also called Cupid, according to which he who loves sows in the flesh; so also there is a certain spiritual love, according to which that inner man who loves sows in the spirit. And to say it more plainly, if there is anyone who still bears the image of the earthly according to the outer man, he is driven by an earthly desire and love. But he who bears the image of the heavenly according to the inner man is driven by a heavenly desire and love.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

quotes.quote: We had indeed already spoken before about the tabernacle, to the best of our ability; but since the description itself is often repeated in the book of Exodus — for it is set forth both when God commanded Moses how it ought to be made, and again when Moses commanded the people to offer materials for the work to be constructed, as this reading contains, which has just now been recited to us; but also afterwards the individual items are enumerated, when they are fashioned by Bezalel and the other wise men, and again when they are brought into the sight of Moses, and once more when they are dedicated by the Lord's command. Moreover, a mention of these things is made also in other books or places, and it is frequently repeated, inasmuch as it is necessarily brought to mind. Now, then, that discourse has been recited to us where it says: "and Moses said to all the synagogue of the sons of…

"You stretched out your right hand, the earth devoured them." The earth indeed devours the impious even today. Or does it not seem to you that the earth devours him who always thinks of earth, who always has earthly deeds, who speaks of earth, disputes about earth, desires earth, and places all his hope in earth? — who does not look to heaven, who does not think of things to come, who does not fear the judgment of God nor desire his blessed promises, but always thinks of things present, and sighs after things earthly? When you see such a man, say that "the earth has devoured him." But also if you see anyone given over to the luxury of the flesh and the pleasures of the body, in whom the mind avails nothing, but the lust of the flesh has taken possession of the whole, say also of this one that "the earth has devoured him." It still moves me that he says: "you stretched out your right…

"This is my God, and I will honor him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him." This one, then, is both "my" "God" and the God "of my father." Our Father, who made us and begot us, is Christ, and he himself says: "I go to my Father and your Father, my God and your God." If, therefore, I recognize that God is "my" "God," I will glorify him; but if I also recognize this, in what way he is the "God" of Christ "my father," I will exalt him: for it is a loftier understanding, in what way Christ, in order to bind fast and safeguard the truth of the one God, calls him his God whom by nature he calls Father.

The first commandment, then, is: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me". And after this there follows: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness, whatever things are in heaven above and whatever are in the earth below and whatever are in the waters under the earth; you shall not adore them nor worship them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the sons, unto the third and fourth generation, upon those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and who keep my precepts". All these things together some suppose to be one commandment. But if it be so supposed, the number of ten commandments will not be filled out—and where then will be the truth of the Decalogue? But if it be divided in the manner in which we too distinguished it in the utterance above, the whole number of ten commandments will…

In Matthew it is not written: "he was beginning"; but here, because he was about to ascend from baptism, "he was beginning" is read, Scripture relating: "and this same Jesus was beginning". For when he was baptized and took up the mystery of the second birth, so that you too might destroy your former nativity and be born in the second regeneration, then he is said "to have begun". And just as the people of the Jews, when they were in Egypt, did not have a beginning of months, but when they had gone out of Egypt, then it is said to them: "this month, the beginning of months, shall be the first for you among the months of the year", so he who is not yet baptized is not narrated "to have begun". For let us not suppose that it was added in vain to that which is said, "this same was Jesus", what follows: "beginning".
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 28

quotes.quote:
But now we shall pass to the text itself, word by word, so that the meaning inherent in the historical events may be shown more rationally. The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: "This month is for you the beginning of months, the first for you among the months of the year."

God says to Moses and Aaron, as they come out of Egypt, that this is the beginning of months and the first among the months of the year. As regards the historical sense, then, this is indeed the first month, and the Jews celebrate this feast every year on the fourteenth day of the first month, when they sacrifice a lamb in their houses according to the Law given to them through Moses. Yet since Christ came "not to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to bring them to fulfillment," He has shown us what the true Passover is, the true passage out of Egypt.

It is the beginning of months for the one…

But let us now proceed to what follows in the pericope: "Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel: On the tenth day of this month let each one take a lamb for every family, let each one take a lamb per house."

He does not say, "Let them sacrifice a lamb on the tenth of the month," but "Let them take a lamb." They are commanded to sacrifice this lamb on the fourteenth day of the month, and it is in this way that the Hebrews celebrate the Passover. They must, then, take the lamb in every house and in every family beginning from the tenth day, feed it still on the eleventh, the twelfth, and the thirteenth day, and finally consecrate it with a prayer: "This lamb is offered in sacrifice for this and this reason," without neglecting the eighteen names. On the fourteenth day, between the two evenings, the lamb is immolated, so that five are the days that intervene from the…

But meanwhile Jethro comes to Moses, bringing with him his daughter, the wife of Moses, and his sons. "And Aaron came" it says "and all the presbyters of Israel, to eat bread with the father-in-law of Moses in the sight of God". Not all eat bread "in the sight of God", but those who are "presbyters", who are elders, who are perfect and proved by their merits, they eat bread "in the sight of God"; those who observe that which the Apostle says: "whether you eat, or drink, or do anything else, do all to the glory of God". Everything, therefore, that the saints do, they do "in the sight of God"; the sinner flees from the sight of God. For it is written that Adam, after he sinned, fled "from the sight of God" and, when questioned, answered: "I heard" he said "your voice, and I hid myself, because I was naked". But Cain too, after he was condemned by God for fratricide, "went out" it says…

"But if two men should be fighting and strike a pregnant woman, and her infant should come forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss, as much as the woman's husband shall impose, and he shall pay with honor. But if it be fully formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise." First of all, in these matters, I think we must inquire under what heading of the law statutes of this kind are reckoned. For it is not, as it seems to the simpler sort, that everything which is enacted is called "law"; rather, some things are indeed called law, some testimonies, others commandments and acts of righteousness, and some are called judgments. This the eighteenth Psalm teaches more plainly, gathering them together in one place, when it says: "the law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the…

But let us see what is said to Moses after these things, what way is enjoined to be chosen. "From Othon," it says, "turn back and make your journey between Epauleum and Magdolum, which is over against Beelsephon." Now these are interpreted thus: "Epauleum" indeed a winding ascent, "Magdolum" a tower, "Beelsephon" the ascent of a watchtower, or having a watchtower. You perhaps believed that the way which God shows was level and soft and had absolutely no difficulty or labor: it is an ascent, and a winding ascent. For the way by which one strives toward the virtues is not downhill, but one ascends, and ascends narrowly and with difficulty. Hear also the Lord in the Gospel saying how "strait and narrow is the way that leads to life." See, then, how greatly the Gospel agrees with the Law. In the Law the way of virtue is shown to be a winding ascent; in the Gospels it is called "the strait…

But if there are any who have gone out of Egypt, and, having followed the pillar of fire and cloud, have come into the wilderness, he descends to them from heaven, furnishing them a minute and subtle food, like to that of the angels, so that man eats the bread of angels.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 1

quotes.quote: Because, therefore, he had advanced so far in understanding as to recognize his own self—in which lies the greatest part of wisdom—the divine favor rewards him. Hear with what rich and magnificent gifts. "I," he says, "will open your mouth, and will instruct you in what you ought to speak". Blessed are those whose mouth God opens, that they may speak. To the prophets God opens the mouth and fills it with his own utterance, as he says in the present passage: "I will open your mouth and will instruct you in what you ought to speak". But through David also God says: "Enlarge your mouth, and I will fill it". Likewise Paul too says: "that speech may be given me in the opening of my mouth". The mouth, therefore, of those who speak the words of God, God opens. But I fear that there may be some whose mouth, on the contrary, the devil opens. For whoever speaks a lie, it is certain that the devil…

If anyone should worthily understand either the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt or the crossing of the Red Sea, and indeed this whole road that is traveled through the desert and each of the several encampments of the camp; if he should prove so capable of these things that he even receives the law of God "written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God"; if anyone, I say, should so come to these things through the order of the journeyings, that, fulfilling each one in the spirit, he attains also those increases of the virtues which are indicated in them, then he can consequently arrive also at the vision and understanding of the tabernacle. Concerning this tabernacle the divine Scriptures make mention indeed in many places and seem to indicate certain things which human hearing could scarcely be capable of; yet above all the Apostle Paul, concerning the understanding of…

It is added after these things that "he too with whom imperishable woods were found", brought them to the Lord. If anyone "loves Christ the Lord in incorruption", he offers imperishable wood to God. Blessed, therefore, is he with whom is found either an incorrupt understanding or an incorrupt body, and offers this to God. Hence too he said very well: "with whom imperishable woods were found". For "imperishable woods" are not found with everyone. Of gold he did not say, nor of silver, with whom it was found; for understanding and speech can be found with everyone. But neither did he say this of the four colors; for it belongs to all to consist, according to the body, of four elements. But "imperishable woods", that is, the grace of incorruption and virginity, can be found with only a rare one, as the Lord too says: "not all receive this word, but those to whom it is given".
Rams' skins also are offered. Certain men before us have also set the ram for fury. And because the skin is a token of a dead animal, he who offers rams' skins to the Lord shows fury dead in himself.

After these, sores and blisters with burning are brought forth in the sixth blow. And it seems to me that in the sores there is convicted deceitful and festering malice, in the blisters swelling and inflated pride, in the burning the madness of anger and fury. Thus far the torments are tempered to the world through the figures of its own errors.

The princes also offer oil, to serve for a twofold use, for the lamps and for the anointing. For the lamp of those who preside over peoples ought not to be hidden or "put under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house". But the princes also offer "the composition of incense", which is to be compounded by Moses "for a sweet odor to the Lord", so that they too may say that "we are a good odor of Christ".

And yet what does he say? Let us see how or how far he bids us set out from Egypt: "we will go," he says, "a journey of three days into the wilderness, and there we will sacrifice to the Lord our God". What is "the way of three days" which we must travel, that, going out from Egypt, we may be able to arrive at the place in which we ought to sacrifice? I understand that way to be he who said: "I am the way, the truth, and the life". This way must be traveled by us in three days. For whoever "shall confess with his mouth the Lord Jesus and shall believe in his heart that God raised him from the dead" on the third day, "shall be saved". This, then, is the "three days' way" by which one arrives at the place where one may sacrifice to the Lord and render "the sacrifice of praise". This, as far as pertains to the mystical understanding. But if we seek also the moral sense, which is most…

But since God is truly the "instructor of infants" and the "teacher of the foolish", He corrects faults and amends errors, and He says to Moses that he should take the rod and, striking the rock, bring forth waters for them. For He wishes them now to drink "from the rock", He wishes them to advance and to come to the inner mysteries. For "they murmured against Moses", and therefore the Lord commands that Moses show them a rock from which they may drink. If there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law which is written according to the letter displeases him, because in many things it does not seem to preserve consistency, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, that he may drink from there and refresh his thirst. But this rock, unless it be struck, will not give waters; but when struck it brings forth fountains. For Christ, when struck and…

One must not therefore eat the flesh of the lamb raw, as the slaves of the letter do in the manner of animals which are irrational and quite savage. In relation to men who are truly rational through their desire to understand the spiritual aspects of the world, the former [slaves of the letter] share the company of wild beasts.We must strive, however, in transforming the rawness of Scripture into boiled food, not to transform what has been written into what is flaccid, watery and limp. This is what they do who "have itching ears and" turn them away "from the truth" and transform the anagogical meanings so far as they are concerned to the carelessness and wateriness of their manner of life.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.103-4

quotes.quote:
Once we have been anointed — that is, once we have believed in Christ — then we are given the command to approach the food of Christ, as the words that follow clearly show: "They eat the flesh roasted with fire this night, and they feed upon the unleavened bread set on bitter herbs. You shall not eat of a lamb raw or boiled in water, but roasted with fire, the head with the feet and the entrails."

[…] If Christ is the lamb, and if Christ is the Logos, what is the flesh of the divine words if not the divine Scriptures? It is upon these very Scriptures that we ought fittingly to feed, when they are neither raw nor boiled. If some make a superficial use of these words, they would be feeding upon the flesh of the Savior raw; and, precisely because they partake of His flesh raw, they would procure for themselves not life but death, inasmuch as they eat of His flesh like wild beasts and not…

"For the cavalry of Pharaoh entered with chariots and riders into the sea, and the Lord brought the water of the sea upon them; but the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea." And you too, if you are a "son of Israel," can walk "on dry ground in the midst of the sea"; if you are "in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation like the light of the sun, holding the word of life unto glory," it can come to pass that, as you walk in the midst of sinners, the moisture of sin does not soak you; it can come to pass that, as you pass through this world, no wave of lust bespatters you, no heat of desire beats upon you. But he who is an Egyptian and follows Pharaoh is drowned in the waves of the vices. But he who follows Christ and, as he walked, so walks himself, for him the "waters" become "a wall on the right hand and on the left," while he himself goes forward on the…

That the activity of the Father and the Son is to be found both in saints and in sinners is clear from the fact that all rational beings are partakers of the word of God, that is, of reason, and so have implanted within them some seeds, as it were, of wisdom and righteousness, which is Christ. And all things that exist derive their share of being from him who truly exists, who said through Moses, "I am that I am"; which participation in God the Father extends to all, both righteous and sinners, rational and irrational creatures and absolutely everything that exists.

Although making a variety of suppositions about him, we all know something of God but do not all know what he is, for few indeed and fewer (if I may say so) than few are they who grasp his holiness in all things. Thus we are rightly taught to pray that our concept of God may be hallowed among us. Thus we shall see his holiness in creating, in providing, in judging, in choosing and abandoning, in accepting and rejecting, in rewarding and punishing each one according to his merits.In these activities and others like them is found, so I may say, the stamp of the personal character of God, that which in my opinion is called in Scripture the "name of God." So in Exodus: "You shall not take the name of your God in vain."

At the last the destruction of the firstborn is brought on, in which there is perhaps something above our understanding, namely what seems to have been committed by the Egyptians against "the church of the firstborn, which is enrolled in heaven". Whence too the destroying angel is sent to a ministry of this kind, to spare only those who shall be found to have both doorposts marked with the blood of the lamb. Meanwhile the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed, whether we say they are the "principalities and powers" and "the rulers of the darkness of this world", whom Christ at his coming is said to have "led forth", that is, to have led captive "and to have triumphed over on the wood of the cross"; or whether we say they are the authors and inventors of the false religions which have been in this world, which the truth of Christ has extinguished and destroyed together with their…

I will yet set down one testimony concerning stones, since indeed in the canticle of Exodus it is written: "let them be turned into stones, until your people pass over, O Lord, until this your people pass over, whom you have possessed". And so God is asked that for a little while the Gentiles be turned into stones—for the Greek word sounds this more pointedly, "ἀπολιθούντωσαν" (let them be petrified)—"until the people" of the Jews "pass over". There is no doubt that, after those have passed over, the Gentiles will cease to be stony and, in place of a hard heart, will receive in Christ a human and rational nature: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 22

quotes.quote: "Let them become like stone, until your people pass over, O Lord, until this your people pass over, whom you have acquired." "To become like stone" is not to be by nature a stone; for it would not become that which it was not. This we say on account of those who say that Pharaoh or the Egyptians were of an evil nature and were not led into these things by the freedom of the will; and also on account of those who accuse God the creator as savage, because he turns men into stones. Let these, therefore, before they blaspheme, consider with the utmost weighing the things that are written. For he did not say "let them become like stone" and fall silent, but he set a time and decreed a measure of the condemnation. For he says: "until your people pass over," namely so that after the passing of the people they may not be "like stones." In which it seems to me that something of prophecy lies…

After this it is written: "in the second month", it says, "after they had set out from Egypt, on the fifteenth day of the month, the people murmured against Moses, saying: would that we had died in the land of Egypt, when we sat over the pots of flesh and ate bread to our fill, for you have led us out into this desert, to kill the whole synagogue with hunger". Granted, for the correction of readers let the sin of the people be indicated, that it murmured and was ungrateful for the divine benefits, when it was receiving the heavenly manna; but why is even the day written, on which day "the people murmured"? "In the second month", it says, "on the fifteenth day of the month"; which surely is not written without reason. Recall the things which were said concerning the laws of the Passover, and you will find that this is the time which is appointed for keeping the second Passover by those…

"If they were too few in one house to be sufficient for eating a lamb, he shall take to himself his neighbor, the one nearest. And each shall measure, upon a lamb, what is sufficient for him, reckoning the number of persons. Let the lamb be for you perfect, male, and a year old. You shall take it from among lambs and kids" […].

Each one must associate to himself the neighbor nearest to his house, so that the guests may be sufficient for the lamb, that is, the number of persons is counted for one lamb.

"A perfect lamb, male, a year old." For Christ is perfect because He is lacking in nothing and, in Himself, is in nothing imperfect. Male refers to His strength and His courage. He is called "a year old" because a year indicates a perfect number, inasmuch as in the space of twelve months the sun returns to its seat.

Those who eat do not feed in the same way but differently, each…

To the advantage of these last salvation has come, thanks to His blood, the blood of Christ, the perfect lamb; for "as a lamb He was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb silent before its shearer, so He opens not His mouth. Who shall tell of His generation? For His life is taken away from the earth, and for the iniquities of His people He was led to death. And I will give the poor in exchange for His death and the rich in exchange for His tomb, because He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth." For His death was not caused by sin, but He Himself "bears our sins and is afflicted for us; by the blows He suffered we were healed."

As those of old were prefigured in a male lamb, so are we in a man like a lamb; as they were in a perfect lamb, so are we in the fullness of the will of the Father; as they were in a lamb of one year, so are we in the completion of the ages — for…

Moses, when he had seen the bush burning and not consumed, marveling at the sight said: "I will pass over and behold this sight." Certainly he too was not signifying that he would traverse some span of earth, nor climb mountains nor go apart into the steep places of the valleys. The vision was close to him, in his mouth and in his eyes. But he says: "I will pass over," to show that, admonished by the heavenly vision, he ought to ascend to a higher life and to cross over from those things in which he was to better things.

Great, then, is the vision, when God is seen with a pure heart. Great is the vision when with a pure heart the Word of God, and the Wisdom of God, who is His Christ, is acknowledged. Great is the vision, to acknowledge and to believe in the Holy Spirit. Great, then, is this vision — the knowledge of the Trinity. Nevertheless, even Moses was then seeing in Exodus the great vision, and he who was seen in the bush in the fire is called an angel, and he calls it a great vision. For he understood who it was in the angel. For immediately thereupon He says to God: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob". See, then, how great this vision is — although this very thing also is great, to know that God makes "His angels spirits, and His ministers a burning fire". And now indeed to Moses, still pasturing the flocks of Jethro his father-in-law, and stepping or passing…

Observe that he has named a certain power of the soul feet, with which we as it were make our way, walking toward him who said "I am the way", and which must be shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. And I think that the symbols of these sandals are the "sandals" recorded in Exodus, which those who ate the Passover and were ready for the journey were required to have. For thus he says, "You shall eat it: your loins girded and your sandals on your feet and your staffs in your hands, and you shall eat it with haste; it is the Lord's Passover". For it belongs to readiness both to eat "with haste" and to eat shod, so that, being strengthened by the food, they may be able to journey.

Therefore let him who is journeying be shod, but let him who has arrived at the holy land unloose his sandals; for "Loose", he says, "the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy…

Like to this also is that which is said by God through Moses: "Behold, I have set you in a hole of the rock, and you shall see My back parts." Therefore this rock, which is Christ, is not closed on every side, but has a hole. And the hole of the rock is that which reveals God and makes Him known to men. No one, then, sees the Father except the Son; no one, then, sees the last things of God — that is, the things which come to pass in the last times — except one placed in the hole of the rock, namely when he has learned those things by the revelation of Christ.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 4

quotes.quote: For it is well known that he, that is, the one who gave the oracles to Moses, says, "You shall not see my face but my back." Certainly these statements must be understood by the aid of that symbolism which is appropriate to the understanding of divine sayings, and those old wives' fables, which ignorant people invent on the subject of the front and back parts of God, must be utterly rejected and despised. Nor indeed must anyone suppose that we have entertained some impious thought in saying that the Father is not visible even to the Savior, but he must consider the exact meaning of the terms we use in controverting the heretics. For we have said that it is one thing to see and be seen, another to perceive and be perceived or to know and be known. To see and be seen is a property of bodies, which it would certainly not be right to apply either to the Father or to the Son or to the Holy…

After these things let us see what the second commandment also seems to contain: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness of the things that are in heaven or that are in the earth or that are in the waters under the earth". Idols are one thing, and gods far another, as the Apostle himself likewise teaches us. For concerning gods he said: "as there are many gods and many lords"; but concerning idols he says: "for an idol is nothing in the world". Hence it seems to me that he read what the law says not carelessly. For he saw the difference between gods and idols, and again the difference between idols and likenesses; for he who said of idols that they do not exist did not add that likenesses also do not exist. But here it says: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor a likeness of any things". It is one thing, then, to make an "idol", another to make a "likeness".…

Abraham sets forth, as it were, moral philosophy, through obedience. For so great was his obedience and observance of the commandments that, when he heard: "Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from the house of your father," he did not delay, but did it at once … For hearing that he should sacrifice his son, not even then does he doubt, but he obeys the precept: and, to give to posterity an example of the obedience which is moral philosophy, he did not spare even his only son. Isaac also holds to natural philosophy, since he both digs wells and searches out the depths of things. But Jacob too holds the inspective place, inasmuch as he was named Israel on account of the contemplation of divine things, and saw the camps of heaven, and beheld the house of God and the ways of the angels — that is, the ladder stretched out from earth to heaven.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

quotes.quote: God has been recorded indeed to be the God "of Abraham, and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." He indeed who wishes the light to belong to none other than men (because it is said, "The life was the light of men") will think, according to this analogy, that the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob is the God of no one except these three fathers alone. But he is at least also the God of Elijah, and, as Judith says, the God of her father Simeon, and he is God of the Hebrews. Wherefore, according to the analogy, if nothing prevents him from being the God of others also, nothing prevents the light of men from also being the light of other creatures besides men.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2.143

quotes.quote: If the God of the universe, having been made familiar to the saints, becomes their God, the being named the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, by how much more will it be possible for the Holy Spirit, having been made familiar to the prophets, to be called their spirit, that the Spirit might thus be said to be the spirit of Elijah and the spirit of Isaiah?
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.68

quotes.quote: The males which were holy from the fact that they had opened their mother's womb were offered before the altar of the Lord: "every male," it says, "that opens the womb", sounds something sacred. For whatever male you may say has been poured forth from the womb, he does not open his mother's womb as the Lord Jesus does, because in all women it is not the birth of the infant, but the intercourse of the man, that unlocks the womb. But the womb of the Lord's mother was unlocked at that time at which the birth also was brought forth, because before the birth of Christ no male at all touched that holy womb, to be venerated with all reverence.
quotes.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

quotes.quote: And God said, "Honor your father and your mother," teaching that the child should pay the honor which is due to his parents. Of this honor to parents one part was to share with them the necessaries of life, such as food and clothing, and if there was any other thing in which it was possible for them to show favor toward their own parents.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11.9

quotes.quote: And again, who would deny that the command which says, "Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you," is useful quite apart from any spiritual interpretation and that it ought certainly to be observed, especially when we remember that the apostle Paul has quoted it in the same words?

The saying is taken from Exodus, running thus: "Honour your father and your mother, that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you." And here, in setting out the wording, the Apostle has left out the "your" (after 'mother'), and instead of "and that you may be long-lived" he has made it and you shall be long-lived, and he has left out, after upon the earth, the "which the Lord your God gives you."

But it is the fifth commandment of the Decalogue; therefore it must be asked how one ought to understand the which is the first commandment, since the first commandment is stated to be "You shall have no other gods besides me." Now some have read which is the first commandment with a promise in this way, as though the commandments before it did not contain a promise; for they think that upon this one there lies for the first time…

"The Lord who crushes wars, the Lord is his name." I would not have you think that the Lord "crushes" only visible battles, but he "crushes" also those which are for us "not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world." For "the Lord is his name": and there is no creature of which he is not Lord.

But what does Scripture say? "The midwives feared God," it says, "and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them." Certain men before us have said that these midwives hold the pattern of rational learning. For midwives are, as it were, in the middle, and tend both the males and the females at their birth. This learning, then, of common rational knowledge reaches to nearly every faculty, instructs all, tends all. If anyone in it be of manly spirit and wish to seek heavenly things and to pursue divine things, he will come, as though healed and warmed by learning of this kind, better prepared for the understanding of divine things. For there is one, as it were the sparrow, which teaches the loftier things and, with the rational wings of doctrine, summons souls to fly on high. The other, which is ruddy or modest, is moral, orders behavior, teaches modesty, instills honesty. To me,…

But meanwhile let us see what the present history now unfolds: "Moses went up" it says "to the top of the hill". He does not yet go up to the top of the mountain, but "to the top of the hill". For it was reserved for him to go up to the top of the mountain then, when Jesus was to go up, and Moses with Him, and Elijah, and there be transformed into glory. Now, therefore, as one not yet glorified from the transformation of Jesus, he does not go up to the top of the mountain, but "he goes up to the top of the hill".

A reading from Exodus has been recited to us, one that may either spur us on to the search for understanding or drive us back from it. It spurs on minds that are studious and free; it drives back those that are idle and preoccupied. For it is written: "Aaron and all the sons of Israel saw Moses, and his face was glorified and the color of his countenance, and they were afraid to approach him." And a little after: "Moses," it says, "placed a veil over his face. But when he entered into the sight of the Lord, to speak with him, he laid the veil aside." Now the Apostle, expounding these things with that magnificent understanding which he employs in the rest, of which he said: "but we have the mind of Christ," says: "for if the ministry of death, formed in letters upon stones, was in glory, so that the sons of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his…

First of all, then, let us see what it is that Moses says to the sons of Israel: "take from among your own selves a redemption for the Lord; everyone who has conceived it in his heart, let him offer the first offerings to the Lord". Moses does not wish you to offer to God something that is outside you: "from your own selves", he says, "take, and bring the first offerings to the Lord, according as each one has conceived it in his heart". Gold and silver are commanded to be brought, bronze and the other materials; how can I bring this from my own self? Surely gold is not born within me, or silver and the other things that are commanded? Does not each one bring these forth from his storerooms and from his chests? What is it, then, that Moses says: "bring from your own selves, and each one according as he has conceived it in his heart"? That gold indeed and silver and the other materials,…

But not to Moses only is it promised that his mouth shall be opened by the Lord, but to Aaron also. For it is said concerning him too: "I will open your mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you are to do".

But, as I see, Jethro did not come to Moses in vain, nor in vain did he eat bread with the elders of the people "in the sight of the Lord". For he gives Moses counsel quite fitting and useful, that he should choose men and appoint as princes of the people "men who worship God, mighty men and hating pride". For such ought the princes of the people to be, who are not only not proud, but even hate pride, that is, that they should not only themselves be without vice, but should also hate vices in others; I do not say hating men, but vices. "And you shall appoint them" it says "as tribunes and centurions and leaders of fifty and leaders of ten, and they shall judge the people at every hour. But the matter that is weightier, they shall refer to you". Let the princes of the people and the presbyters of the plebs hear that they ought to judge the people at every hour, always and without ceasing…

"The nations heard and were angry; pangs seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Then the leaders of Edom hastened, and the princes of the Moabites; trembling took hold of them. All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away." As far as pertains to the history, it is established that none of these nations was present at the marvels which were done; how, then, will they seem to be terrified with trembling, or to have "hastened," as he says, or the "Philistines" and "Moabites" and "Edom" and the rest of the nations which he enumerates, to be "angry"? But if we return to the spiritual understanding, you will find that "Philistia" — that is, falling peoples — and "Edom," which is interpreted earthly, tremble, and the princes of all these run about and are afraid, gripped by pangs, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, penetrated by him "who descended into the lower parts of the earth,"…

But we can also derive another understanding from these things. If you flee Egypt, if you leave the darkness of ignorance and follow the Law of God, Moses, and the sea meets you, and the wave of those who contradict runs against you, do you strike the struggling waves with the rod of Moses—that is, with the word of the Law and the vigilance of the Scriptures—and by disputing open for yourself a way through the adversaries; the waves will give way at once, and the conquered surges will yield place to the victors, and while those who a little before were opposing you marvel and are astonished and are fixed in stupor, you, along the lawful lines of disputations, will cut the straight way of faith and will make such progress by the word of teaching that your hearers, whom you have instructed by the rod of the Law, may themselves now rise up against the Egyptians like the waves of the sea,…

What shall we say about the rest? For they are many, and to discuss each one is a huge task. But what will it profit, that they be spoken with our own huge labor, yet be spurned and perish, spurned by preoccupied hearers who attend upon the word of God for scarcely the point of a single hour? For "unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it". Nevertheless we, as has already been said above, deliver the Lord's money to the table; let each one of the hearers see how he receives the things that are delivered. "Let each one", he says, "according as he has conceived it in his heart, bring the first offerings to the Lord". As for what he called "first offerings", I ask what are the first offerings of gold, or what the first-fruits of silver? And how do first-fruits seem to be contributed from scarlet and purple and fine linen? Or how does one offer "according as…

"But there arose", it says, "another king in Egypt, who knew not Joseph. And he said to his people: behold, the race of the sons of Israel is a great multitude, and is stronger than we". First of all I wish to inquire who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who is the one who knows him not. For while that one reigned who knew Joseph, the sons of Israel are not reported to have been afflicted, nor consumed "in clay and brick", nor were their males killed and their females kept alive. But when that one arose who had not known Joseph and himself began to reign, then all these things are reported to have been done. Who then is this king, let us see. If the Lord governs us, and the sense of our mind, illuminated by the Lord, always holds the memory of Christ, doing that which Paul writes to Timothy: "be mindful that Christ Jesus has risen from the dead" — while he remembers these…

"Seeing," then, these of the tribe of Levi "that the infant was comely, they concealed him for three months. And when they could no longer conceal him, his mother took," it says, "an ark and daubed it with bitumen and placed the infant in it and set it in the marsh beside the river. And his sister watched from afar, to see what would happen to him. But the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself in the river, and she heard the infant crying, and she sent," it says, "and took him up, and the daughter of Pharaoh said that this is of the infants of the Hebrews." After this it is then related how his sister spoke, that she might call the mother of the boy to nurse him. "And the daughter of Pharaoh said to her," it says, "keep this infant for me, and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages. And when she had nursed him, as he grew stronger, she brought him to the daughter of…

"The teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth," the Apostle Paul, handed down to the Church which he gathered from among the Gentiles how it ought to attend to the books of the Law, which it had received from others and which had formerly been unknown to it and altogether foreign, lest, in taking up institutions foreign to it and being ignorant of the rule of those institutions, it should tremble amid an alien instrument. Therefore he himself, in a number of passages, hands down examples of the understanding, so that we too may observe things similar in the rest, lest perchance, on account of the likeness of the reading and of the instrument of the Jews, we should believe that we have been made their disciples. This, then, is what he wishes to distinguish between the disciples of Christ and the disciples of the synagogue: that the Law which they, by understanding it badly, did not…

"Raising themselves up," it says, "the children of Israel came from Rameses to Succoth, and departing from Succoth they came to Othon." If there is anyone who is preparing to depart from Egypt, if there is anyone who desires to leave behind the dark deeds of this world and the darkness of errors, first of all he must depart "from Rameses." Now "Rameses" is interpreted the commotion of the moth. If, therefore, you wish to come to this, that the Lord may be your leader and go before you "in the pillar of the cloud" and that the rock may follow you, which may furnish you "spiritual food" and no less "spiritual drink," depart and go out "from Rameses," "and do not lay up treasure there, where the moth destroys and where thieves dig through and steal." This is what the Lord openly says in the Gospels: "if you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have…

We must also inquire who that being was of whom it is said in Exodus that he wished to kill Moses because he was setting out for Egypt. And afterwards, who is it that is called the "destroying angel," and who also is he who in Leviticus is described as Apopompeus, that is, the Averter, of whom the Scripture speaks thus: "One lot for the Lord, and one lot for Apopompeus"?

We partake of the flesh of Christ, that is, of the divine Scriptures, […] we strive to follow in the footsteps of the true lamb, for the Apostle declares that Christ is the lamb of our Passover when he says: "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed." His flesh, His bones, and His blood, as has already been shown, are the divine Scriptures: if we eat them, we possess Christ, inasmuch as His bones have become words, and the thoughts that arise from the words, flesh. If we approach them as is fitting, we contemplate what is to come "in an enigma and as through a mirror," for His blood is the evangelical faith of the new covenant, as the Apostle testifies when he says: "profaning the blood of the covenant." Anointed with this blood, that is, with faith, we shall escape the destroyer.

After this the gnats are brought forth. This animal is indeed suspended by its wings, flitting through the air, but it is so subtle and minute that it escapes the sight of the eye unless one sees sharply; yet when it has settled on the body, it bores in with a most bitter sting, so that the one whom a man is not able to see flying, he feels stinging. This kind of animal therefore I think most fittingly compared to the art of dialectic, which bores through souls with minute and subtle stings of words and circumvents them with such craftiness that the deceived man neither sees nor understands whence he is deceived.

Yet the third day is always made fitting for sacred mysteries. For when the people had gone out of Egypt, on the third day it offers sacrifice to God, and on the third day it is purified; and the resurrection of the Lord is on the third day; and many other mysteries are enclosed within this day.

[God] warns a man inclined to idolatry not to practice it. But when a man who is not so inclined but yet through cowardice, which he calls "accommodation," pretends to worship idols as the masses do, he does not, it is true, worship idols, but he does bow before them. And I would say that they who abjure Christianity in the courtroom or even before they are brought there do not worship idols, but they do bow down before them; for they apply to inanimate and unheeding matter the name of the Lord God, namely "God".

It is obvious that the Jews follow the law where God is represented as saying, "You shall have none other gods but me; you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness of anything in the heaven above and in the earth beneath and in the waters under the earth; you shall not bow down to them nor worship them." And they worship none other than the supreme God who made heaven and everything else. It is clear then that since those who live according to the law reverence him who made the heavens, they do not reverence the heavens together with God. Furthermore, none of those who serve the Mosaic law worship the angels in heaven. And in the same way that they do not worship the sun, moon and stars, "the world of heaven," they avoid worshiping heaven and the angels in it.

Christians and Jews are led to avoid temples and altars and images by the command "You shall fear the Lord your God and him only shall you serve." … And not only do they avoid them, but when necessary they readily come to the point of death to avoid defiling their conception of the God of the universe by any act of this kind contrary to his law.

When men try to seduce us to apostasy, it is useful to reflect upon what God wishes to teach us when he says, "I am the Lord your God, jealous." In my view, just as the bridegroom who wishes to make his bride live chastely so as to give herself entirely to him and beware of any relationship whatever with any man other than her husband, pretends, though he be wise, to be jealous—he uses this pretense as a kind of antidote for his bride—so the Lawgiver, especially when he reveals himself as "the firstborn of every creature," says to his bride, the soul, that he is a jealous God. In this way he keeps his followers from any fornication with demons and pretended gods.

Now Christ is especially jealous for the house of God in each of us, not wishing it to be a house of merchandise or that the house of prayer become a den of thieves, since he is Son of a jealous God. This is the case if we understand such words from the Scriptures in a reasonable manner, which were spoken metaphorically from the human viewpoint to set forth the fact that God wishes nothing alien to his will to be mingled with the soul of any, but especially with the soul of those who wish to receive [the teachings of the] most divine faith.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.221

quotes.quote: He adds, moreover, and says: "you shall not adore them nor worship them". To worship is one thing, to adore another. A person can sometimes adore even unwillingly, as some, flattering kings, when they have seen them given over to devotions of this kind, feign that they adore idols, though in their heart it is certain that an idol is nothing; but to worship is to be enslaved to these things with the whole affection and zeal. Both, therefore, the divine word cuts away, so that you neither worship with affection nor adore in outward show. Yet it must be known that, when you have resolved to keep the charge of this precept and to repudiate all the other gods and lords, and to have besides the one God and Lord no one as either god or lord, this is to have declared war without treaty upon all the rest. When, therefore, we come to the grace of baptism, renouncing all other gods and lords, we…

"For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God". See the kindness of God, how, in order to teach us and make us perfect, he himself does not refuse the frailty of human affections. For who, hearing of a "jealous God", would not straightway wonder and think it a fault of human frailty? But God both does and suffers all things for our sake, and, that we may be able to be taught, he speaks in affections known and familiar to us. Let us see, then, what this is that he says: "I am a jealous God". But that we may more easily be able to contemplate things divine, let us be taught by human examples, according to those things we discoursed of above. Every woman is either under a husband and subject to the laws of the husband, or is a harlot and uses the liberty of sinning. He, therefore, who goes in to a harlot knows himself to have gone in to a woman who is prostituted and lies open to all who…

After this it says that: "they came to Elim, and there were there twelve fountains of waters and seventy palm trees". Do you suppose it has no reason that the people is not led first "to Elim", where "there were twelve fountains of waters", in which there was no bitterness, but rather where there was very great pleasantness from the density of the palms, but is led first to salt and bitter waters, which, being made sweet through the tree shown by the Lord, one afterward comes to the fountains? If we follow the history alone, it does not much edify us to know to what place they came first and to what second; but if we search out the mystery lying hidden in these things, we find the order of faith. For first the people is led to the letter of the law; from this, so long as it remains in its bitterness, it cannot depart; but when it has been made sweet through the "tree of life" and the…

But when the passage about the equipment of the tabernacle is read, believing that the things described therein are types, some seek for ideas which they can attach to each detail that is mentioned in connection with the tabernacle. Now so far as concerns their belief that the tabernacle is a type of something they are not wrong. But in rightly attaching the word of Scripture to the particular idea of which the tabernacle is a type, here they sometimes fall into error.

"Who," he says, "is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you? Glorious among the saints, wonderful in majesties, working prodigies." When he says "who is like you among the gods?", he does not compare God to the idols of the nations, nor to the demons who falsely claim for themselves the name of gods, but he calls those gods who are called gods through the grace and participation of God. Concerning whom Scripture also says elsewhere: "I said: you are gods," and again: "God stood in the assembly of the gods." But these, although they are capable of God and seem to be granted this name through grace, yet none is found like to God either in power or in nature. And although John the Apostle says: "little children, we do not yet know what we shall be; but if he shall be revealed to us" — speaking, of course, of the Lord — "we shall be like him," yet this likeness is referred not to…

This "king, who did not know Joseph," devises many things against the people of God, and is forever seeking new arts of doing harm. But now his cunning surpasses all measure, when through the ministry of the midwives he attempts to destroy the offspring of that people — by the very art through which life is usually preserved. For what does he say? "And the king of the Egyptians said," it says, "to the midwives of the Hebrews, to one of them whose name was Sephora, and the name of the other was Phua, and he said: when you deliver the Hebrew women and they are near the birth, if it be a male, kill him; if a female, let it live." But to these words there is joined in what follows: "but the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they let the males live." If the things that are written were to be taken according to the narrative of the history, then…

This Pharaoh, who is the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself more vehemently pressed to let the people of God go, in the second place desires to obtain this, "that they should not go far off", that they should not set out the whole three days, and he says: "do not go far off". The matter is carried on not by words only; blows follow too—he orders the scribes of the Hebrews to be scourged, straw not to be given, the work to be exacted; these things the fathers endured, in the figure of whom the people of God also, which is in the Church, often suffers as well. For you will find, if you consider them, that those who have wholly handed themselves over to "the prince of this world" act with prosperous successes, that everything, as they themselves think, turns out happily for them; but that to the servants of God often not even these humble and small things of human sustenance turn out well. For these things I think seem to be the straw that is furnished by Pharaoh. Hear, then, now also the kind of sanctification: "do not approach" it says "a woman today and tomorrow, that on the third day you may hear the word of God". And you too, therefore, if you withdraw from the Egyptians and flee from the power of demons, see how great the helps are that are divinely prepared for you, see how great the helpers are whom you employ. But who is so blessed that he so disburdens himself of the weight of temptations that no thought of uncertainty creeps into his mind? See what is said by the Lord to that great foundation of the Church and most solid rock,…

"O Lord, who reign unto the age and unto the age and still." As often as "unto the age" is said, a length of time indeed is indicated, but some end; and if it is said unto another age, there is set, without doubt, some longer end, yet an end; and as often as "the ages of the ages" are named, perhaps, though unknown to us, yet some limit appointed by God is indicated. But that which he added in this place, "and still," left no sense of any limit or end. For whatever you conceive, in which you think an end can consist, the prophetic word always says to you: "and still," as if it should speak to you and say: do you think the Lord will reign unto the age of the age? "And still." Do you think "unto the ages of the ages"? "And still." And whatever you say of the spans of his kingdom, the prophet always says to you: "and still."

But also, when she has become worthy that it may be said of her as it was said of Moses, that "Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him," then is fulfilled in her that which He says: "Make me hear your voice." … But a great praise of her is shown in what is said: Your voice is sweet. quotes.quote: "And it came to pass" it says "that when Moses raised his hands, Israel became superior". Moses indeed raises his hands, he does not stretch them out; but Jesus, who, lifted up on the cross, was to embrace the whole circle of the earth with His arms, says: "I have stretched out my hands to a people that does not believe and that contradicts me". Moses, then, raises his hands, and when he raised his hands, Amalek was conquered. To raise the hands is to raise one's works and deeds to God, and not to have one's deeds cast down and lying on the ground, but pleasing to God and lifted up to heaven. He raises his hands, therefore, who "lays up treasure in heaven"; for "where his treasure is", there also is his eye, there also his hands. In truth, the feast here set before us is properly named in Hebrew not "Passover" but "phas," of which the translation is "passage" (for the three letters of "phas," together with the more forceful rough breathing among the Hebrews, make up the name of this feast). Since, then, it was on the occasion of this feast that the people of Israel came out of Egypt, it is consequently called "phas," that is, "passage."

quotes.quote: But that in the fifth place Egypt is beaten by the slaying of the animals or cattle, in this there is convicted the madness and folly of mortals, who, like irrational cattle, imposed the worship and the name of God upon the figures not only of men but also of cattle, stamped upon wood and stones, venerating Ammon-Jupiter in a ram and Anubis in a dog, worshipping Apis also in a bull, and the rest of the monstrous gods which Egypt marvels at, so that in the very things in which they believed a divine worship to reside, in these they might see pitiable torments.

But just as we read written that "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing", so we too cannot be satisfied in beholding and considering the things that are written, from how many sides they build us up, in how many ways they instruct us. For indeed, when I perceive that Moses, a prophet full of God, to whom God spoke "face to face", received counsel from Jethro, a priest of Midian, I fall into an amazement of mind out of exceeding wonder. Wherefore we…

This is without doubt what he shows: that so long as anyone remains in the dark deeds of the world and is engaged in the obscurity of affairs, he cannot "serve the Lord"; for he cannot "serve two masters", he cannot "serve the Lord and mammon". These, then, who are doubtful and are worn out in tribulations, even speak against Moses and Aaron and say: 'from the day you go in and go out to Pharaoh, you have made our odor abominable before him.' In Exodus something of this kind is written: "and it came to pass after many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God". As long as Pharaoh lived, the "children of Israel" did "not groan", and, placed under punishments, they did not even have the free faculty of "groaning"; for the king was alive, who commanded them to make "bricks and straw". As long as Pharaoh lived, they did "not groan to God"; when Pharaoh died, then they had the strength to lift up their faces wet with weeping. The wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the devil lives. Then we labor at "bricks" and "straw", then we swallow our tears in silence and do the first works of iniquity; but when he has died, at the visitation of the Lord our God, then we "groan to the Lord".
After having inflicted the Egyptians with many plagues, he led them out of Egypt in the month of flowers, when the most pleasant spring appears and the sadness of winter passes away.

This, I say, is the first month of the year. This brings joy to every creature. It clothes the naked trees. It opens the earth. This produces joy in all animals. It brings mirth to all. This is for Christians Xanthicus, the first month, the time of the resurrection in which their bodies will be glorified by means of the light which even now is in them hidden. But if man groans and cries out to God, he sends him the spiritual Moses, who redeems him from the slavery of the Egyptians. quotes.quote: … Jesus Christ was to introduce the second people (which is composed of us nations, lingering deserted in the world previously) into the land of promise, "flowing with milk and honey" (that is, into the possession of eternal life, than which nothing is sweeter). This had to come about not through Moses (that is, not through the law's discipline) but through Joshua (that is, through the new law's grace), after our circumcision with "a knife of rock" (that is, with Christ's precepts, for Christ is in many ways and figures predicted as a rock). Therefore the man who was being prepared to act as an image of this sacrament was inaugurated under the figure of the Lord's name, even so as to be named Jesus.

But why was it that [Christ] chose twelve apostles, and not some other number? In truth, I might from this very point conclude of my Christ that he was foretold not only by the words of prophets but by the embodied language of facts. For of this number I find figurative hints up and down the Creator's dispensation in the twelve springs of Elim; in the twelve gems of Aaron's priestly vestment; and in the twelve stones appointed by Joshua to be taken out of the Jordan and set up for the ark of the covenant.

But what parts of the law can I defend as good with a greater confidence than those which heresy has shown such a longing for—as the statute of retaliation, requiring eye for eye, tooth for tooth and stripe for stripe? Now there is not here any smack of permission to mutual injury. There is rather, on the whole, a provision for restraining violence. To a people which was very obdurate and wanting in faith toward God, it might seem tedious and even incredible to expect from God that vengeance which was subsequently to be declared by the prophet: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord." Therefore, in the meanwhile, the commission of wrong was to be checked by the fear of retribution immediately to happen. So the permission of this retribution was to be the prohibition of provocation. In this way a stop might thus be put to all hot-blooded injury. By the permission of the second…

But, to come now to Moses, why, I wonder, did he merely at the time when Joshua was battling against Amalek, pray sitting with hands expanded, when, in circumstances so critical, he ought rather, surely, to have commended his prayer by knees bent, and hands beating his breast, and a face prostrate on the ground; except it was that there, where the name of the Lord Jesus was the theme of speech—destined as he was to enter the lists one day singly against the devil—the figure of the cross was also necessary, [that figure] through which Jesus was to win the victory?

For Joshua was to introduce the people into the land of promise, not Moses. Now he called him an angel on account of the magnitude of the mighty deeds which he was to achieve (which mighty deeds Joshua the son of Nun did, as you can yourselves read) and on account of his office of prophet announcing the divine will. Similarly the Spirit, speaking in the person of the Father, calls the forerunner of Christ, John, a future angel, through the prophet: "Behold, I send my angel before your"—that is, Christ's—"face, who shall prepare your way before you."

He called him an angel indeed, because of the greatness of the powers which he was to exercise and because of his prophetic office, while announcing the will of God. He is called Joshua (also Jesus), because it was a type of his own future name.

In this passage, he teaches him the art of educating. And well he might, for it was through Moses, in fact, that the Lord of the ancient people was the educator of his children. It is in his own person, however, face to face, that he is the guide of the new people.

It is said in the ode, "For he has triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider has he cast into the sea." The many-limbed and brutal affection, lust, with the rider mounted, who gives reigns to pleasures, "he has cast into the sea," throwing them away into the disorders of the world. Thus also Plato, in his book On the Soul, says that the charioteer and the horse that ran off—the irrational part, which is divided in two, into anger and concupiscence—fall down. For he who was able to prophesy is not to be thought to have spoken without foresight. Since he was more inclined to devotion toward God the Creator, and knew that he was revered by the Egyptians because of the administration through which he governed Egypt in a time of great famine, after his departure he sought to have this error removed: he was sure of the vanity of the crowd, which honors the dead more like gods than the living, so that the honor due to the Creator would not be given to him. Therefore he showed that he was free from the vain superstition of the Egyptians, when he ordered his bones to be carried elsewhere so that they would not…

quotes.quote: IF, WHEN JOHN OR THE SAVIOR WAS PREACHING, THE LAW CEASED, HOW DOES THE SAVIOR SAY, “I HAVE NOT COME TO DESTROY THE LAW OR THE PROPHETS, BUT TO FULFILL” (Matt. 5:17)? FOR IF IT HAS BEEN FORBIDDEN, HOW IS IT NOT ABOLISHED, SINCE IT HAS LOST THE AUTHORITY TO BE CARRIED OUT? — Everything that was spoken about Christ has been fulfilled; and the Lord Himself therefore fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, since He did everything that was written about Him, and did not dissolve anything, but confirmed it. For the Law and the Prophets were until Him. The Prophets spoke about Him; therefore beyond Him, what was said by them about this, namely, about Christ, cannot extend; nor after Him could the Prophets find anything of this sort, because they have neither one to speak about, and He about whom it was spoken has already come. Indeed they encompassed in their books all things: His incarnation, His…
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 69: ON CHRIST FULFILLING THE LAW

quotes.quote: What shall we say of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose end, such as it was, lies before our eyes as an act of vengeance (Gen. 19:24)? It came to pass that all, stained with the disgrace of every kind of filth, were consumed by divine fire. In the Flood all were under one fate, so that all perished with one death and at the same time, except the household of Noah (Gen. 7). And the whole army of Pharaoh would have to be said to have been born under a single decree, so that the foolish error of astrology might be punished, since they were drowned in the Red Sea with their king (Exod. 14:24). And how many other great examples there are which we pass over, because two examples are enough for our purpose; how much more, then, with so many mysteries?
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 115: CONCERNING FATE

quotes.quote: THERE WAS NO OTHER SIGN THAT MOSES PERFORMED OPENLY BEFORE PHARAOH EXCEPT THE SERPENT (Exod. 7:10) — Whoever considers this blameworthy should say what else ought to have been done. For indeed he made a serpent, which both inspired terror yet did not harm, because it is somewhat slow to injure due to a certain stupor. For if he had made a lion, or a bear, or something of that sort, how would those present have escaped? He did not wish to kill anyone, but only to instill fear and to show power; so that since the first transgression began through a serpent, in like manner the calling to mind of the knowledge of God and the correction of conduct might come through the sign of a serpent, so that as sin came about, so it might also be corrected. Just as sin came through a woman, so it was taken away through a woman, namely Mary, the Mother of the Lord, from whom Christ was born and condemned…
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 8: ON THE SERPENT MOSES MADE BEFORE PHARAOH

quotes.quote: WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT GOD, WHO IS PROCLAIMED AS JUST, HAS PROMISED TO REPAY THE SINS OF THE FATHERS UPON THE CHILDREN TO THE THIRD AND FOURTH GENERATION? — Anyone who doubts that God does nothing and says nothing unjust is out of his mind. Therefore, if the words of the Lord are not suppressed, but everything that relates to this same question is set forth, what seems obscure will come to light, and what is thought hardly just will be recognized as devout. For whoever suppresses the words of a question is either ignorant or shifty, preferring accusation to teaching. Further, the Lord indeed promised that He would repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, but upon those who hate Him, that is, those who, involved in their fathers’ evils, have served idols just as their fathers did. For he is an enemy of God who transfers the honor of His name to a creature. Just as the sons of the…
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 14: ON REPAYING THE FATHERS' SINS UPON THE CHILDREN

quotes.quote: WHAT DOES THIS SAYING MEAN, “MAN ATE THE BREAD OF ANGELS”, WHEN ANGELS DO NOT NEED FOOD, SINCE THEY ARE SIMPLE BY NATURE AND ENDOWED WITH SPIRITUAL POWER? — The bread that he calls “of angels” is manna. Now manna is interpreted as “What is this?” For when the children of Israel saw something like white coriander seed fall upon the ground, they said to one another, “What is this?” (Exod. 16:15). In the Hebrew language this is called “MAN HU.” This bread or food, therefore, was not created by the law of the world, by a mixture of elements; but it came from above, provided by a spiritual ordering. Nor indeed was it kept in the heavens beforehand, since it was created by the power of God in a moment for the nourishment of bodies. It was called, however, the bread of angels because it was created by that same power by which angelic nature survives and lives. For without God there is no life.…
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 20: ON THE BREAD OF ANGELS

quotes.quote: CAN SOULS, THEN, BE TRANSLATED JUST LIKE BODIES? — I think it is dishonorable to say that souls are generated together with bodies, so that a soul is born from a soul, a thing that does not belong even to the soul itself. Or if indeed each of the heavenly powers was made individually, and from them the rest came to be, then it might seem believable that from the one soul of Adam the other souls are born. But this is not fitting, because this was possible for God alone, that the simple should generate, and was not granted to others. This is so mysterious in the case of the Savior that it is considered unbelievable not only by pagans or Jews alone, but even by those who call themselves Christians. For the Photinians and Arians reject this faith and do not believe that God has generated. For if at the time when the body is sown the soul also is generated from a soul, we read that a rib was…
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 23: CAN SOULS BE TRANSLATED JUST LIKE BODIES?

quotes.quote: HOW IS IT PROVED THAT THE SAVIOR ROSE FROM THE DEAD AFTER THREE DAYS AND NIGHTS? — In this matter, if you seek the number of days and nights in strict sequence, you will gain no true understanding. For Moses fasted forty days and forty nights (Exod. 34:28), and yet a complete numerical count is not found: for when he went up by day and came down by day, he clearly did not fulfill the entire number; but because where there is day, night is also reckoned, and where there is night, day is likewise counted, so that the part is taken for the whole, they are called forty days and forty nights. Therefore it is with what the Savior said: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12:40). And because there are three nights, three days are also to be taken. Night is indeed something that might seem new or…
quotes.source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 64: ON THE THREE DAYS AND THREE NIGHTS

quotes.quote: WHY WERE CIRCUMCISION AND PRECEPTS GIVEN TO THE PEOPLE, WHICH PREVIOUSLY DID NOT EXIST AND NOW ARE NO LONGER HELD IN AUTHORITY? — Circumcision is a sign of Abraham’s faith, so that when this sign was seen in his sons, it might be known that they were his sons, who, believing God, had received this sign (Gen. 17:10–11). But the commandments about Sabbaths and things past were given as testimony, and about things to come which were to have a figure (Exod. 20:9–11). For the future Sabbath, in which He will grant rest in eternity, is foreshadowed by this Sabbath that was made in the completed week. The law of foods, however, was not given at the beginning of the Law, but when, under a leader, they were faithless and did not want to give faith to God’s words and promises, they received, because of the hardness of their heart, precepts that were not good, as the prophet Jeremiah says (Ezek.…
